in writing. − centres of excellence (ce) are scientific units or organisational structures that carry out scientific research and develop advanced technologies at the highest world level. they bring together teams of scientists with outstanding research achievements who collaborate on common themes, carry out joint research and technology projects, work closely with industry and conduct training and education activities. the cds should be organisationally independent by design, but at the same time they must be based on a recognised research unit (this could be, for example, a pan, a university or a research and development unit). the centre of excellence programme does not envisage the creation of new research institutions, but rather a kind of 'laboratory' actively collaborating with industry or other scientific centres. the researchers working within the centre address strategic issues by drawing on the scientific facilities of several different institutions, working under a common scientific and organisational direction, with a relatively high degree of autonomy. centres of excellence should carry out both basic and applied research projects and participate in the implementation of innovative technologies. the size of the team and the available research facilities must be sufficient to carry out the planned work.
in writing. − the mep, as part of his work in a parliamentary committee, reports on the draft text of a legal act presented by the european commission, which has the sole legislative initiative. the parliamentary committee shall put the report to the vote, with any amendments that may be necessary. the european parliament shall express its position by amending the text and voting in plenary. the adoption of legislative acts is governed by the ordinary legislative procedure (co-decision), which places parliament on an equal footing with the council, and by special legislative procedures, which apply only to specific cases where parliament has a consultative role. on certain matters, the european parliament has only a consultative role. in some cases, the treaty makes consultation mandatory because it is required by a legal basis, in which case the draft cannot become law unless parliament delivers an opinion. in such a situation, the council shall not be empowered to take a decision on its own. parliament has the right of political initiative. it may request the commission to submit draft legislative acts to the council. parliament is effectively involved in the development of new legislative texts, as it considers the commission's annual work programme and indicates the acts that should be adopted. most european laws are passed jointly by the european parliament and the governments of the member states. the legislative workflow is called the ordinary legislative procedure.

in writing. - this report, drawn up by our colleague, the chairman of the parliament's committee on international trade, concerns the alignment of council regulation (ec) no 774/94 opening and providing for the administration of certain community quotas for certain meat and cereals products with the 'lisbon' legislative system, namely articles 290 and 291 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. regulation (ec) no 774/94 confers implementing powers on the european commission and gives it the possibility to adapt its provisions as regards the size of tariff quotas and their conditions. the amendments we, as meps, wish to make to this regulation include the european parliament in the preparation and implementation of delegated acts by providing us with full documentation from the meetings on the drafting of acts at expert level, limit the delegation of powers to the commission to five-year periods and extend the deadline for the possible objection to acts, if any. i fully support these proposals, because they will give the european parliament the right to have an insight into the work of the commission and the international trade committee, with its corresponding powers, will have control over the procedures relating to quotas.
in writing. − union tariff quotas are established to ensure that a certain set of goods can be imported into the european union at customs duties lower than those recorded in the customs tariff. the exhaustion of a union tariff quota or the expiry of a period for which it is established shall not automatically block the possibility of importing from third countries. the import of the goods is still possible, but the customs office will then use the rate set in the customs tariff, and not in the regulation establishing the union tariff quota, to calculate the value of the duty due. in the case of union tariff quotas, the type of goods for which these preferential trade policy measures are established is essential to the way in which they are allocated. the main division is between agri-food commodities and what are conventionally called industrial commodities (conventionally because fish, for example, also belong to this group). agri-food products are goods covered by the common agricultural policy, which is governed by community legislation, and processed goods not covered by annex i to the treaty establishing the european community, so-called non-annex i goods. industrial goods are all other goods subject to customs duties.
in writing. - imports from turkey are becoming increasingly popular. although this is not as popular as, say, imports from china, it seems that turkey could soon become the largest factory in the old continent. no, it's not a mistake in the previous topic article, we explained why turkey should be understood (especially in terms of imports) in terms of a european country. now, following the punch, we begin the cycle of answering questions from e-import.pl readers. the first concerns customs clearance, a problem for many importers importing goods from turkey. in the broad sense, trade with turkey (and therefore imports from turkey) is based on the customs union legislation, which is fully complemented by free trade agreements. the latter concern unprocessed agricultural products and products covered by the treaty establishing the european coal and steel community (whose competence has now been taken over by the european union). these legal resolutions, which regulate the rules of trade between the community countries and turkey (which is seeking accession to the eu), provide for and constitute the total abolition of import and export duties on the union-turkey line. in addition, the provisions provide for the abolition of other charges, including those of an internal nature, which may not be levied on industrial goods imported from turkey and covered by the provisions of the customs union.

in writing. − the use of carbon capture and storage technology in european industry is currently the only method that is expected to lead to significant co2 emissions reductions in industrial sectors such as steel, cement, chemicals and oil refineries. this method, using carbon dioxide from the combustion of fossil fuels, contributes to the production of low-carbon electricity and has an impact on the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. the implementation of this technology is of particular importance in view of the european union's objective of significantly reducing co2 emissions by 2050. moreover, according to the international energy agency, fossil fuels will continue to dominate energy markets in the coming decades, which further increases the importance of the technology. i think we should invest in new, low-carbon, environmentally friendly technologies and promote them. one of them is the method of carbon capture and storage used by european industry. however, it should be borne in mind that it still requires specific guidance from the european commission to obtain financial support for its implementation in individual member states.
in writing. − carbon capture and storage technology can be one of the key elements in reducing carbon emissions into the atmosphere. unfortunately, its implementation faces a number of technical and financial problems. the number of pilot schemes so far is small, and transporting carbon dioxide from the point of emission to the place of storage is a major environmental challenge. it should be stressed that, in a situation where it is clear that these technologies are far from being implemented, the role of biological sorption, including in soils, in reducing the level of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere should also be considered. actions to increase it could lead to effective carbon offsetting.
in writing. − the deployment of carbon capture and storage (ccs) technology will be of key importance in the coming years, given that global co2 emissions will need to be significantly reduced by 2050. this technology is the only one capable of producing substantial co2 reductions, as it is suitable for keeping the global temperature rise below 2°c. in this way, we could counter the threat of global warming.
in writing. − the development of renewable energy sources should remain a key objective of legislation, but also of eu financial support. carbon capture and storage should be considered as a transitional solution that can help to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from industrial sources. this technology cannot be considered as competitive with renewable energy sources and cannot be considered as a means of reducing co2 emissions. however, its proper implementation and closing the legal gap should make it much easier for member states to introduce new, cleaner energy technologies.
in writing. - a few decades ago, carbon capture and storage (ccs) emerged as a breakthrough technology that would enable fossil fuel-based power plants to be powered without further environmental damage. but the work on co2 sequestration has been accompanied by disappointed hopes and unfulfilled promises from the start. in theory, ccs technology allows carbon dioxide to be captured, transported and compressed underground, where it is stored safely and does not escape into the atmosphere. in practice, stopping carbon dioxide emissions from fossil fuels used for energy production and other industrial purposes is proving very difficult and expensive. while some of the carbon capture and storage processes are already being used successfully, for example in natural gas extraction, the development of an integrated system to capture co2 on an industrial scale, for example in fossil fuel-fired power plants, is still in the future. despite many incentives from governments around the world to develop carbon capture and storage technologies, many projects never got off the drawing board because of the huge investment and uncertainty about future profits. the projects that are still underway require huge support from the state and there is no guarantee that the invested funds will ever be returned.
in writing. − this project complements the first plan adopted in 2004 to promote the use of ict in european healthcare systems. given the adverse demographic changes currently taking place, such as the ageing of the population, the increase in the incidence of chronic diseases, the decrease in the number of medical staff and the increasing demands on the quality of medical services, i believe that ehealth is a tool to ensure easier and equal access to healthcare for all citizens. this is particularly useful for people with chronic illnesses who can be treated at home or who live in remote or sparsely populated areas. the introduction of ehealth services also has the clear advantage of providing easy access to personalised patient medical records stored in one place, regardless of where the patient is currently located. however, it is necessary to guarantee an adequate level of security and protection for union citizens' personal data and medical data, which can be relatively easily targeted by hacking and attacks. i believe that the successful implementation of the ehealth action plan 2012-2020 also requires close cooperation between local and regional authorities to secure eu grants for innovative health policy solutions in individual member states.

in writing. − while progress has been made since 2004, when the eu launched the first ehealth action plan, obstacles to the configuration of an integrated european system still exist, including: lack of knowledge and trust among patients, citizens and healthcare professionals about ehealth solutions; lack of interoperability of ehealth solutions; inadequate or incomplete regulatory framework; regional differences in access to ict services and limited access in the most deprived areas. the high number of incompatible products in europe is an inevitable consequence of market fragmentation and the absence of standards for communication and exchange or the fact that mass buyers are not familiar with these standards. as a result, it is often not possible to connect the it systems of countries, border regions or even health centres. for example, software used in the radiology departments of some hospitals cannot be linked to software used in other departments of the same hospital. in line with the objectives of the europe 2020 strategy and the digital agenda for europe, the new action plan aims to identify and address these obstacles, clarify policy issues and provide a concise overview of ehealth in europe. the global e-health market, which is undergoing a huge expansion, could be worth $27.3 billion by 2016. some of the major european companies are world leaders in this field.
in writing. - i supported a draft report on the food crisis, fraud in the food supply chain and its control. the agri-food industry is a fast-growing sector of the european economy, employing 48 million people. i believe that ensuring food safety is one of the european union's top priorities. in this context, the union has a very detailed legal framework on the need to carry out controls at different stages of the food supply chain, but there is no uniform definition of fraud in the food sector. unfortunately, recent experience shows that there is an increasing incidence of food counterfeiting, including the substitution of main ingredients for cheaper and inferior counterparts, mislabelling of products or labelling of ordinary food as organic. recent european-wide fraud scandals include the sale of horse meat as beef, caged eggs as organic eggs, and road salt as table salt. the european union should therefore make every effort to minimise the scale of fraud in the food sector. to this end, the frequency of unannounced checks and inspections by the commission's food and veterinary office should be increased, as well as the cooperation at international level between the relevant national authorities and europol in cases of cross-border investigations.

in writing. − the presence of equine animals in meat sold as beef on the european market demonstrates the existence of deficiencies in the food control system and the unreliability of food producers and distributors. we must make a clear stand against this kind of behavior. we are investing too much in european agriculture, ensuring that farmers and processors meet high quality standards, only to have confidence in our food sector eroded by the dishonest practices of traders looking for profit at any cost. i am in favour of making the eu food chain more transparent, taking into account the need for legislative changes towards increased traceability of products and their ingredients, so that the consumer has clarity on where the food they buy really comes from. this will involve a review of the way food is labelled. more frequent, random checks are also needed at different stages of the food chain, taking into account the transnational nature of the process. on the one hand, we must therefore try to harmonise the rules on controls between member states and ensure that information flows smoothly. on the other hand, i would call for the centralisation of food safety agencies within each member state, in order to clearly define their responsibilities and improve their functioning. furthermore, i believe that the crisis in question is a great opportunity to look more closely at the benefits of short, local production chains. for these reasons, i fully support the report presented.
in writing. − the new fraud cases uncovered in the food sector show that fraud is a growing problem, with an increasingly diverse nature, and that new ways of detecting and punishing fraud are needed to eliminate illicit profits. the first priority should be to ensure that food quality standards are respected. on the one hand, the increasing number of exposed frauds, such as the horse meat scandal or the sale of ordinary products as organic, shows that consumer safety is increasing and fraud is being exposed. on the other hand, the knowledge that road salt may have been present in everyday food products raises legitimate concerns among consumers. it is not easy to detect counterfeit food before it is placed on the market. it's hard to prevent fraud. but when it does, many people may be harmed by eating food that does not conform to the label. let us not forget that the main reason for fraud in the food industry is not to poison consumers, who are also customers of food producers, but to gain economic advantage. it should lead to a situation where producers are not paid to cheat themselves and other companies, reducing consumer confidence in the product. we also need a clear definition of food fraud and crime, and strong penalties can act as a deterrent.
in writing. - the biggest problem is the issue of counterfeiting food products. a rigid legal framework is needed in this area. counterfeit food products are being placed on the market, which may endanger the general consumer. the european union should start pushing for new legislative solutions. specific actions should be regulated and public confidence in the institutions should be increased. sanctions are far from intimidating, and we need to increase penalties for economic fraud. food safety and the interests of consumers have always been the primary concerns of the envi committee and of the european parliament as a whole. in recent years, there has been increasing attention to the related but distinct issue of fraud in the food sector, for example in relation to cases of fraudulent food labelling and other fraud that have affected the eu food supply chain. examples such as the use of road salt for food, the sale of normal eggs as organic, and the recent horse meat scandal seem to indicate a persistent or structural problem. such cases of food fraud have negatively affected consumer confidence in the food supply chain, creating a major paradox: food is safer than ever, but consumer confidence is low.

in writing. − a worker's company is one of many types of company in an economy. it is situated within a general legal and organisational framework and has certain characteristics which clearly distinguish it from other companies. before discussing these characteristics, it is necessary to identify the factors that characterise the companies in general. the following are the main features of a partnership. a company is a legal relationship in the form of a contract involving at least two entities pursuing a common economic objective. the company's business may be in the sphere of production, services and trade. a shareholding in a company is linked by law to a share in the company's profits. benefits of participation may include access to certain benefits and services. from an economic point of view, a company is an association of persons or capital for the purpose of carrying on a business. in the broadest sense, a company can be defined as an association of natural or legal persons who pool their capital to carry out a joint economic activity and generate income. the basic division of companies is related to their legal basis. a company formed and operating under the civil code is called a civil company, while a company formed and operating under the commercial companies code is called a commercial company. the following are also distinguished from commercial companies: public company, limited company, limited liability company, joint stock company and their combinations.

in writing. − every citizen of the european union has the right to benefit from social security under eu and national law. access to social protection systems is particularly important in the event of illness, incapacity for work, disability, unemployment or maternity. social benefits help union citizens to adapt to changes in labour markets, while contributing to the fight against social exclusion and poverty. unfortunately, as a result of the economic crisis and the reduction in wages and social contributions, together with the increase in the number of unemployed, the european social protection system has been weakened, and those from particularly vulnerable groups have been the most affected. i therefore believe that member states should develop their own procedures for the development of social benefit systems for their citizens. it is important not to overlook the growing number of selfemployed people, who represent 15% of all those employed in the european union. in some member states, these people often have difficulty in obtaining adequate social assistance. their interests are very rarely represented by trade unions, which further exacerbates the problem of abuses and irregularities. in view of the above, i believe that only effective cooperation between national and eu authorities will be able to effectively tackle the problems arising from differences in labour market legislation.
in writing. − social protection aims to provide men and women with basic income security and access to essential services throughout the various phases of their lives. while they are an essential mechanism for promoting inclusion and addressing inequalities, national social security mechanisms in all member states have been subjected to cuts due to the financial crisis. paradoxically, these cuts took place at the same time as the number of people out of work and in need of social support significantly increased. with the goal of providing lasting and effective social protection for all, the current report calls on member states to optimise and modernise protection systems, ensure sustainable long-term financing for their schemes, and draw up social security strategies that take account of the international labour organisation guidelines. the report further emphasises the need to recognise and protect self-employed workers who, although they represent 15% of the total workforce in the eu generally, have restricted access to social security in some member states. as a socialist mep, i believe that the use of resources for social protection should not be regarded as expenditure but as an investment in sustainable economic growth and social inclusion in the eu. therefore i voted in favour of the report.

in writing. − there is currently no clear eu-wide definition that clearly distinguishes between selfemployed persons who are acting in good faith and are actually selfemployed and fictitious selfemployed persons. each competent authority and institution applies its own legal or regulatory framework, which may vary according to its area of competence and the policy area in which it operates (e.g. taxation, social security, commercial law, labour market, insurance). these abuses may involve the avoidance of social security and tax payments, the violation of workers' rights, or unregistered work. this constitutes a serious distortion of the conditions of competition for the self-employed, micro-enterprises and smes. in its 2006 green paper 'modernising labour law to meet the challenges of the 21st century', the european commission asked whether, in order to facilitate the good faith transition from employment to self-employment and vice versa, greater transparency is needed in the legal definitions of employment and self-employment that are in force in the member states. the consultation on this green paper recognised that the lack of an eu-wide definition could cause problems, particularly in cases of crossborder work (and crossborder provision of services).
in writing. − self-employment is becoming more and more popular, especially among young people, in various forms. in europe, selfemployed people now account for over 15% of all employees, or 33 million people. in poland, this group of people is also growing, not always because they want to take advantage of this opportunity. unfortunately, this form of employment is also used to underpay and circumvent workers' rights. these abuses sometimes involve the avoidance of taxes and social security contributions or lead to unregistered work. in my view, however, it is important to note that in practice there are very different situations with self-employment, sometimes it is the only source of income, but sometimes it is an additional source of income for the employed person. in my opinion, this should affect the obligation to pay not only taxes but also contributions. this requirement should in particular apply to persons for whom self-employment is the sole source of income. lack of social security coverage even from the lowest wage in a country can have serious consequences in the future. we must build europe's legislation in such a way that it provides social protection for all, including the growing number of selfemployed.

in writing. − the incineration of plastic bottles, films, plastics of all kinds and waste poses a major threat to the environment and, above all, to human health. waste incineration is the release of gases and dust into the atmosphere, including carbon dioxide and heavy metals. the combustion of waste such as pvc tiles, plastic buckets and pelvic floor boxes in natural conditions (at low temperatures) produces furans and dioxins, amongst others, which are the most toxic chemical synthetics known to man, while 1 kg of polyurethanes, such as those found in sponges, seals or soles, produces 30 to 50 litres of hydrogen cyanide, or prussic acid, one of the most potent poisons. the dioxins produced by the combustion of plastics are chemicals that are dangerous even in trace amounts - they are 10,000 times more toxic than potassium cyanide than, say, tcdd. these compounds are carcinogenic, mutagenic, disrupt the structure of the genetic code, lower immune resistance, impair growth, and cause neurological and hormonal disorders, miscarriages and allergic rashes. the toxic effects of these compounds are slowly damaging many internal organs, such as the liver, kidneys, spinal cord and cerebral cortex. awareness of the harmful effects of releasing waste products into the atmosphere in unsuitable facilities, and warning others, can save us all from the worst of all possible illnesses.

deputising for the rapporteur. − mr president, i will speak in english. unfortunately mr juvin, our rapporteur on the concession directive, cannot be here today as we have just heard. he very much apologises that he is not available, due to unforeseen circumstances. he asked me to take the floor on his behalf to share with you a few thoughts, once again ahead of the vote tomorrow on the concession directive and the two public procurement directives. regarding concessions, the rapporteur would like to emphasise that this directive creates a brand new legal framework at eu level. the vote tomorrow in plenary on the concession text will be a strong signal in favour of the reinforcement of the internal market, filling in the gaps left in the legislative framework. the rapporteur, mr juvin, insists on the fact that it was indeed time to take action at eu level: firstly, to clarify the legal framework throughout the eu in view of the multiplication of case law and of the diverging interpretations of key notions between our member states; secondly, to ensure legal security and stability, which is essential for all actors; thirdly, to support public authorities’ action in favour of the development of economic infrastructure and the promotion of public services, especially in a context of economic crisis and budgetary constraints; and fourthly, to ensure transparency and equal treatment between all candidates and fight potential abuses. however, the legislative proposal as initially proposed by the commission was missing the point. concessions are not public contracts. their specificities must be taken into account: more flexibility, more room for manoeuvre for public authorities and for negotiation. this, however, must be achieved taking due account of the need for transparency and equal treatment. two years have now passed since the proposal was published by the commission. a final agreement was reached in trialogue last july. the final text has been clarified and made more readable, more pragmatic, more efficient and more adapted to the specific nature of concessions, which are mostly long-term, complex contracts, often renegotiated several times with a light approach. the public authoritiesʼ freedom of administration is acknowledged. public authorities are free to decide how best to manage the execution of the works and the provision of the services, and they are never obliged to use concessions. they are the ones who decide how to perform their public tasks. other key principles have been inserted or made clearer, such as transparency, equal treatment, the freedom to define services of general economic interest, etc. the final text ensures key factors to guarantee a healthy economic environment, the transparency of the procedure, and equality of treatment of economic operators, with the same rules applying to everyone. finally, the agreement takes into account the complexities of national situations, for instance in terms of public-public cooperation. two more sentences from mr juvin: the text to be voted tomorrow in plenary has survived despite many misunderstandings and false debates. no, the directive is not going to lead to the privatisation of public services. this was an erroneous and abusive interpretation. the award of a concession is not in itself a privatisation, as concessions do not lead to the definitive sale of an activity by the public authority. and the last sentence from mr juvin, mr president. no, the directive will not lead to low-cost public services. this was raised as the usual bogeyman against any attempt by the eu to legislate. but again those allegations are deceitful, as public authorities remain free to decide how to manage their services, as they are also free to define the award criteria, including characteristics linked to the quality of the services. mr juvin thanks all colleagues, all shadows and all the collaborators and cooperators: thank you very much in his name.

in writing. the amendments to the public procurement directive discussed today set the right direction for the revision of these provisions. the proposal to replace the lowest price criterion with the most economically advantageous offer criterion deserves particular support. this change will result in the exclusion from the tendering procedure of those tenders in which the costs of carrying out the investment have been drastically underestimated in order to obtain the contract at the lowest price. the lowest price criterion not only restricted competition on the market but also in many cases made the final execution of the investment almost impossible, precisely because of the unnaturally low costs. therefore, the introduction of the criterion of the most economically advantageous tender, the significant simplification of tendering procedures and the possibility of submitting tenders electronically will reduce the costs of preparing a tender and will make it easier for many undertakings, especially small and medium-sized ones, to access public procurement. while supporting these amendments, i also call on the commission to make every effort to ensure that the proposed solutions are rapidly implemented in all member states, so that the same rules governing public procurement apply in the community market and that all undertakings, regardless of their size, have the same conditions for participating in tenders.

member of the commission. − mr president, i was going to say that it was not exactly a debate flowing with milk and honey, but i would nevertheless like to clarify certain points. first of all – and i am clarifying these points, because they were mentioned – non-authorised gmo will not be allowed in our food chain. i am saying this because during the debate there was some confusion, with some people saying that we were going to allow non-authorised gmos. so the presence of no non-authorised gmos will be allowed. that legislation already exists, and it will remain. secondly, we are speaking here about a 0.9 % presence of adventitious gmo, that is to say that the presence has to be adventitious for the 0.9 labelling. if it is not adventitious, then the threshold is zero. so each time we refer to labelling and 0.9 % we are referring to an accidental presence of gmo in pollen in honey. now, as was rightly said, i believe by the rapporteur, the real difference from a practical point of view is that, if we consider pollen to be an ingredient of honey, then the 0.9 % of our legislation applies to the pollen. so, when we say 0.9 %, that is 0.9 % of what? if we consider pollen to be an ingredient, then the 0.9 % applies to the pollen, while if we consider pollen to be a natural constituent of honey – as i and the commission believe, and as most of you have said – then you calculate the 0.9 % of the labelling legislation on the honey itself and not just on the pollen. the error which i think some have committed – with due respect – is that first they decide which kind of labelling and which kind of 0.9 % they want, and then they work, illogically, backwards to come to the conclusion that it is an ingredient, while logic indicates that the process should be the opposite. first we decide whether pollen is a natural component constituent or an ingredient, and then we apply the legislation which we already have to that conclusion. as most speakers said, we cannot tamper with nature. i cannot exhibit before you a document indicating what the laws of nature are, because those laws of nature are, by their very nature, unwritten. but the beekeepers say that the pollen is a constituent. those who are in this business say that it is a constituent. so how can we change something which, in the nature of things, indicates that pollen is a constituent? against this argument, some members have pointed out that the court of justice has ruled otherwise. first of all, the court of justice observed that there is no provision in the law which says whether pollen is an ingredient or a constituent. i could have counter-argued that it is the natural way of things; but it took this positivist approach that there is nothing in the law because, had there been an indication – a definition of pollen in the law – as we are determining now, it would have decided otherwise. then, in the absence of a law, the court decided that, in its opinion – even though the codex alimentarius indicates otherwise – it is an ingredient and not a constituent. this does not preclude the legislators of this institution from clarifying this point and saying that, according to the laws of nature, it is a constituent and not an ingredient. so you do not undermine a court judgment because you clarify the law and fill in a loophole which existed before. after all, it is not the court which has to legislate, but the legislator and, as we know, the commission has the exclusive right of initiative in this respect. so, gm pollen needs to be authorised before this amendment of the directive, and after the amendment. there is no change in that. normal labelling rules will apply. they applied before the directive and they will apply after the amendment of this directive. also, as i said before, non-authorised gm will not be allowed at all. in conclusion, let me reiterate that i very much hope to count on the support of the members to open the interinstitutional negotiations as soon as possible. these could then pave the way to a first reading agreement under the greek presidency and during the mandate of this parliament.

in writing. − the european commission submits a legislative proposal to parliament. the parliamentary committee responsible shall appoint a rapporteur member who shall prepare a draft report on the proposal submitted by the european commission. individual members and other parliamentary committees may also be asked for their opinions. the rapporteur presents the draft report to a committee for discussion, after considering the amendments submitted, the draft report is put to the vote in committee, the political groups assess the report in terms of their interests, the report is then discussed in parliament's plenary session and, after any amendments have been made, put to the vote. the adopted document shall state parliament's position on the matter. the european parliament currently has 754 members, elected for five years by direct universal suffrage on the basis of proportional representation. meps are independent parliamentarians, not representatives of individual countries (they are even elected by political group rather than by nationality). they are not bound by any orders or instructions from their own countries and thus enjoy parliamentary privileges and immunities.

in writing. −the security of the eu-russia 'common neighbourhood' depends on many factors. the european union acts as a stabiliser, while the russian federation seeks to maintain a state of destabilisation in order to have greater influence on the six countries of the region. the eu values include democracy, the rule of law and the development of civil societies. the european union through its enlargements in 2004 and 2007 has moved geographically closer to a region of fragile stability, with serious political, economic and security disturbances. on the other hand, these countries are the so-called "near abroad" for the russian federation, which is treated as a buffer zone separating russia from dangerous international phenomena such as terrorism, the expansion of hostile military-political alliances, instability in the middle east region and armed conflicts. the region is therefore a key element of the security policy of the russian federation. the six countries in the eu-russia common neighbourhood are geopolitically disadvantaged, between two powerful international actors with different aims and interests. this affects the security policies of these countries, which have a choice between an alliance with russia (belarus, armenia), euro-atlantic aspirations (ukraine, georgia) or neutrality (moldova, azerbaijan), with foreign policy of these countries depending on internal conditions and these countries quite often change coalitions and priorities in foreign policy (ukraine, moldova).
in writing. − the euro coin series comprises eight different denominations: 1, 2, 5, 10, 20 and 50 cents and 1 and 2 euro coins. each coin has a common side (reverse) and a national side (reverse). the national side indicates the country in which the coin was issued. each of the 16 euro area countries accepts all euro coins, regardless of the denomination and national side. the 'common side' of the coins (reverse) is designed in three designs, depending on the denomination of the coins. all three designs represent a map of europe and symbolise the unity of the european union, and were designed by luc luycx of the royal mint of belgium. the obverse shows the country's national emblem surrounded by the twelve stars of the european union

in writing. − the huge disparities between member states raise doubts about the development of regionalism along european lines. the asean communiqué on the desire to create an aec (asean economic community) by 2020 initially drew positive comparisons with earlier forms of the eu. a closer look at the two organizations, however, reveals numerous structural differences. the eec was a customs union with a leading, supranational body, which meant that the member states delegated control over part of their economies to it. as members of the customs union, the member states have adopted the principles of free trade in respect of all products from other eec countries and have applied a common customs policy towards other countries outside the customs union. but asean countries are not willing to hand over their national economic policies to some supranational body. this means that asean is trying to establish a common market without creating a customs union or any supranational power. moreover, unlike the eu, the political systems of asean countries range from absolute monarchies to military juntas to one-party communist states. with such divergences, political integration of countries like indonesia, malaysia, the philippines, singapore, thailand, and more recently brunei, vietnam, laos, myanmar, seems impossible.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the resolution on tachographs and the social legislation relating to road transport. the proposed regulation amends and updates the 1985 rules on tachographs, which are devices widely used and used in road transport to monitor the working time of drivers. the new entries relate to smart tachographs which will have two additional functions: long-distance communication and recording of vehicle location data. the estimated time to market is 36 months. the regulation provides for an exemption from the obligation to use the equipment in question for lorries of less than 7,5 tonnes used for the transport of materials or equipment for the driver's use within a distance of 100 km from the company's registered office. i believe that the use of new technology in tachographs will minimise fraud, reduce administrative burdens and strengthen social standards.
in writing. - the report by mrs ţicău on the so-called smart tachographs is a good report, linked to the need to replace the 1985 regulation. its main objective is to prevent the manipulation of tachographs, while strengthening the rules on social protection of drivers so that their working and rest times are respected. in addition, the overarching objective is to improve road safety in europe. the so-called smart tachographs are to have two new functions: remote communication for monitoring purposes and the ability to record vehicle location data, which has sparked controversy in the field of data protection. the negotiations with the council were long, but the rapporteur managed to strike a satisfactory balance between improving the working conditions of drivers on the one hand and the issue of data protection on the other. it is thanks to the group of the progressive alliance of socialists and democrats in the ep that the provisions on driver data protection have been included in the document. the negotiated proposal met with my approval.

in writing. - the report adopted today is not only very important for public authorities, but above all it is very good news for businesses. the public procurement procedures are to be simplified, speeded up and cheaper. contracting entities will be encouraged to divide the contract into lots in order to facilitate access to contracts for companies, especially the smallest ones. the proposed simplifications will not only allow large companies to participate in tenders, but also give smes wider access to them. the rules will thus increase the participation of smes in the public procurement market. in working on the package, i stressed that procurement must become more accessible to smes and i am glad that the new rules take this into account. an important change is the provision on the selection criterion, which provides that the lowest price will no longer be treated as the main criterion. the most economically advantageous bid will be selected, not the cheapest. it'll rule out proposals that are cheap because they undercut quality, for example. small entrepreneurs are also exempted from the requirement to provide various types of documents before they enter the procedure. they will also be able to receive information and participate in the tender electronically. i think it's an attractive and less expensive option. i supported the report because it is good for european companies and our economy.

in writing. - we've all had honey at some point. we appreciate its taste and nutritional value, realizing that it is a natural product, extremely healthy and valuable. it is produced by bees that collect and process the nectar of flowers, and the pollen from the plants that reaches it allows the origin of the honey to be defined and to determine whether it is natural or artificial honey. it is pollen that is the main subject of this report. the court of justice of the european union has ruled that pollen is a constituent of honey and not a natural component of honey. it justified this decision by the fact that the honeycombing of honeycombs in the production process could be used by beekeepers to deliberately increase the pollen content of the final product. at the same time, the judgment drew attention to the distinction between honey containing pollen from genetically modified plants and honey containing pollen from non-genetically modified plants. if we were to accept the court's decision, it would require changes in the labelling of honey and costly research to obtain accurate information on the pollen content and origin. this would certainly result in the withdrawal of many beekeepers, especially those who produce honey on a small scale, and in an increase in final retail prices.

in writing. − one of the consequences of the creation of the european union was the abolition of borders between the member states, creating a single market. this has resulted in the european union statistics being deprived of data sources on trade between the countries of the european union, as customs clearance has been discontinued and the sad (single administrative document) has therefore disappeared. a new, common system of statistics on trade in goods between the member states of the european union was needed. the intrastat system has been in force in the european single market area since 1 january 1993. currently, in the member states of the european union, data on foreign trade are derived from two statistical systems that operate in parallel: 1. the extrastat system, which covers the volume of trade of eu member states with so-called third countries, i.e. non-eu member states; 2. the intrastat system, i.e. the statistical system covering trade between eu member states based on data from the intrastat declarations. intrastat is a system for collecting data on trade between member states directly from suppliers and recipients of goods.

member of the commission. − mr president, honourable members, for the commission this has been a reassuring debate. i believe a great majority of this house is united in the rejection of xenophobia, scaremongering and manipulation. i believe we all want to respect the facts, our treaties and each other. several speakers emphasised the mutual benefits of the free movement of workers and also pointed to the fact that actual free movement – cross-border employment and job-seeking – is at a relatively modest level today in the european union. if this is so – if the level of cross-border labour mobility is indeed relatively modest – the question is why some people should think that free movement is a nightmare. setting aside manipulation – and we know there is manipulation, especially when we see certain government officials withdrawing studies because of concern that they would help to clarify the picture for the public – i think this fear probably exists as a result of some unexpected recent developments and also of uncertainty about the future. the unexpected developments include the scale of migration in certain specific cases and certain bad experiences that people in specific localities have had. there has also been uncertainty about the future, but the experience of 1 january 2014, which was recalled by many speakers in this discussion, will hopefully lead to the elimination of that uncertainty, specifically in relation to the free movement of workers from romania and bulgaria. the commission has been working to reduce uncertainty by proposing and implementing concrete measures to ensure that the free movement of workers leads to better outcomes in the future, both economically and socially. we are working for the reinforcement of eures, the european job mobility portal, which i have already mentioned, and i will bring forward the proposal on this very soon. we are also preparing a european platform against undeclared work and, since ms cornelissen mentioned minister asscher, i would point out that he is one of the participants in this effort. together we have looked into such cases and have considered the possibilities for reinforcing labour inspection in the netherlands and using this experience to build the european platform against undeclared work. we have been working on better implementation of the posting of workers directive, which many of the speakers mentioned. i am glad that a good compromise was established in the council in december and i very much hope that in the coming weeks the council and parliament will agree on a good solution. the functioning of this directive will, i hope, lead to better and more services in the eu single market and also to better guarantees against social dumping. we are also working for inclusive growth in source countries, because more opportunities and more jobs need to be created in the more peripheral regions of the union, and we are working for more effective use of the eu financial instruments, especially the european social fund, for this purpose. that point should be highlighted now, at the start of the new seven-year financial period, when countries are still programming the esf allocation. while the discussion has been greatly overheated recently in some countries, it has been quite easy to misrepresent what the commission has been up to in this context. unfortunately this happened last week in the german press, as quoted by ms hirsch, and i would therefore like to point out that certain highly inaccurate statements were circulated in the german press without the commission having said a word about the specific case in question. the first time i spoke about this so-called ‘dano affair’, which is a matter for a court in leipzig, was on monday. i have already clarified the position but, since the report has been repeated, i have to say again that, contrary to what was stated in the german newspaper article, the commission does not generally advocate facilitating the conditions of access to social benefits in the member states, and no case against germany is being taken up by the commission. on the contrary, the commission’s submissions in this context are based on the premise that member states can refuse to grant social assistance allowances to inactive citizens. however, it derives from the case law of the court of justice that this refusal cannot be automatic. the competent national authorities must assess the individual situation of the applicant and, in particular, the period during which the benefit applied for is likely to be granted. if the grant of the requested benefit would place a disproportionate burden on that member state’s social assistance system as a whole, the benefit can be refused. i would like to see quality newspapers in particular paying closer attention to the facts, and if there is a question they should, of course, put it to the commission directly. what happened was disappointing, because i paid specific attention to the situation in german cities that i visited, from munich to hamburg. in many of these places i spoke with the mayors, and i will continue in the coming weeks, in north rhine westphalia, to work with the authorities of cities and regions to find solutions to specific local challenges there. we do not need an escalation of this debate driven by gut feelings. we do not need the kind of bonfire of half-baked ideas which we have witnessed in recent weeks and months. we need more solidarity, more understanding and constructive cooperation to resolve the real problems that exist at municipal level and also at eu level.
vice-president of the commission. − mr president, an overwhelming majority in this house says that freedom of movement is an important positive right for all european citizens without exception. freedom of movement is a right which is also precious to european citizens, because they tell us, in the eurobarometer, that they consider this to be the most important right in the european union. but, like all rights, it comes with obligations. it is up to the member states to take their responsibility and to put these obligations into practice. as my colleague has explained in detail, the commission is ready to give member states a helping hand so that this can be done. the debate has also shown that the commission and parliament are in absolute agreement that freedom of movement is not a problem but an opportunity. it is an opportunity for our economy and for our society. we, as a commission, will make sure it stays so. this house also agrees that free movement is a fundamental right and is not open to negotiation. i can tell you that the commission will make sure that it remains so.
president-in-office of the council. − mr president, honourable members, as i said in my opening remarks, there is very strong and unconditional support in the council for upholding and promoting the principle of free movement as one of the basic freedoms of the eu. i am pleased to take from this afternoon’s debate equally strong support among a very large majority of members of this house. very many of you have called for free movement to be strongly defended. i very much agree, and i consider that both parliament and the council have an interest in working together – of course with the commission – to this end. i also agree with those who have said that we need to have a rational and calm debate on this issue based on facts rather than scare stories. let me conclude by going back to the maastricht treaty of 1993. the treaty of maastricht established the notion of eu citizenship more than 20 years ago. union law and the treaties, as regards citizenship and the rights of citizens, have evolved since then, but one thing has remained the same. free movement of persons is a fundamental right of all eu citizens and their family members, and it is our duty to do our utmost to uphold that fundamental right for the benefit of all our citizens.

in writing. homelessness is a global problem affecting all eu countries. the economic crisis has increased the number of homeless people in denmark, greece, spain, france, poland, the united kingdom, and other countries. between 2011 and 2013, the number of homeless people in poland increased by 19%. combating homelessness requires the cooperation of policy makers, civil society representatives, experts and the homeless themselves. a european strategy to tackle homelessness is to be developed by the end of 2015. it should focus in particular on prevention, which is seven times less costly than addressing the effects of homelessness, and on supporting the development and maintenance of effective national and regional strategies to combat homelessness. in poland, one of the main causes of homelessness is the lack of sufficient affordable public housing. according to finland's experience, housing stability is key to tackling homelessness. in the long term, the finnish 'home first' system is less costly than alternative methods of addressing homelessness in the short term (maintenance of shelters and accommodation, medical care and prevention of the so-called criminalisation of homelessness). the most worrying is the increase in the number of homeless children. there are about 31,000 homeless people in poland, of whom 1,500 are children. most of them are victims of domestic violence. i call on the member states to take special care of this problem in order to prevent the spread of homelessness as quickly as possible.

there is no one scarf and there is no one side of this medal. there is no one value of women's rights. there is also the second value, the value of the life of the unborn, the value of the life of the unborn, and we must speak about this matter calmly, because we are talking about the most important issue. each of us sitting here was once a zygote, an embryo. that's the basic truth. we cannot shout and we cannot embarrass this house with confrontation and aggression. and we must respect the principle that these matters are regulated in the member states. one can be proud to be from a country where abortion is optional. i am a pole, i am proud that human life in poland is protected by law. the constitutional court ruled so. let's respect the difference! europe is one, but each country decides for itself and makes its own laws.
madam president! the european parliament has no reason to debate the availability of abortion in the member states of the european union. this debate is a waste of time and money. but since so many bitter words have been said about spain, i would like to declare on my own behalf that the actions of the spanish government deserve the highest recognition, because abortion, especially abortion on demand, is a barbaric act. we will be ashamed of abortion as we are of slavery today. this is a huge mistake that europe is making. i have two very specific questions to the european commission and to commissioner kallasa: does the commission claim any power to shape the availability of abortion in the eu member states? does the european commission claim any power over the presence of sex education in schools in the eu member states? i'm asking for a legal answer, not a journalistic one.
madam president! the prohibition or restriction of the right to terminate a pregnancy constitutes a form of institutional violence against women. it is an expression of unequal treatment of women and men, discrimination against women, violation of their dignity, health and right to freedom from inhuman and degrading treatment. spain is back to anti-abortion rhetoric, a nod to the catholic church and an attempt to distract from the crisis and the alarming level of youth unemployment. the ban on abortion, it must be remembered, is an attribute of totalitarianism, it was in force under hitlerism, stalinism and francoism. in poland, there is a restrictive anti-abortion law, and its effects are deplorable: there are several hundred legal abortions a year and 150,000 illegal ones. banning abortion doesn't end abortion, it just pushes it underground. the anti-abortion laws are a threat to women's health and lives. they are a form of wealth discrimination, since the abortion ban primarily affects poor women. i call on the spanish people to respect the rights of women and not to follow the polish path, because it is the path of catholic hypocrisy.
madam president! this is not the union we agreed to - a union which interferes with the internal affairs of individual countries, their order, which democratic countries have the exclusive right to regulate, a union which imposes in the sphere of moral action that are unacceptable, that can be considered barbaric. this is not the union we agreed to, and we must therefore be aware that discussions like the one we have today in the european parliament will also arouse anti-union sentiment. we must realise that many europeans want a union, but one in which we can work together while respecting our own particularities, while respecting the exclusive right of each country to determine its own moral standards. we cannot impose our inner convictions on others in matters of conscience, faith and life, because this will not only provoke emotions but also create ever greater divisions and may eventually turn against the european union. remember that.
