in writing. - although the format of the adopted report on the outcome of the committee on petitions' activities in 2013 is not entirely satisfactory to me, its content nevertheless underlines the important role that this committee plays in the development of democratic principles, such as increasing citizen participation in the eu decision-making process and transparency of procedures to ensure that eu law is fully respected. the committee on petitions has devoted more time to debates on environmental issues than to any other sector of activity. in this respect, also thanks to the mission to lower silesia, it was possible for the first time to have the regional authorities hear the complaints of the petitioners against the violation of the result of the referendum on the plans to create a brown coal mine in the legnica deposit. unfortunately, this passage was rejected by the rapporteur, which i do not understand and for which i deeply regret. overall, however, the tone of the report shows the impact of our work in the committee on petitions, where in 2013 the total number of registered complaints approached three thousand, an increase of over 45% compared to 2012, which may be due to the increased legislative powers of the european parliament. we've processed about 1,000 petitions, and only 199 of them have been considered and closed. in this respect, i agree with the rapporteur that the administrative capacity should be strengthened urgently and that clear deadlines for the examination of petitions in the european parliament should be enforced.
in writing. - the increase in the number of petitions to the european parliament by more than 45% compared to 2012 shows that eu citizens are becoming more aware of their rights. the petition is also a tool to increase citizens' confidence in the european union, which has been torn apart by the severe financial crisis. i have informed citizens on many occasions about the possibility of petitioning parliament, and i therefore welcome the plans to develop the online portal of the committee on petitions, which will allow better information about this intervention tool at eu level. citizens should be clearly informed of the scope of the legal competence of the committee on petitions and the reasons for the closure or rejection of petitions should be clearly stated. i welcome the attention drawn by the committee on petitions to the irregularities linked to the non-compliance with the principle of free movement in the eu single market and share the view that more should be done in terms of coordination and alignment of the legislation of individual member states in this area.
in writing. - petitions are dealt with by one of the european parliament's standing committees the committee on petitions. if the petition is found admissible, the committee on petitions may take such action as it considers appropriate in relation to the subject matter of the petition. these may include: • presenting a report to parliament for a vote in plenary; • forwarding petitions to other committees which may take them into account in their legislative work; • requesting the european commission to carry out a preliminary inquiry into the compatibility of the legislative acts covered by the petition with eu law. but the petition does not provide for the possibility of obtaining compensation. the european parliament also does not take any binding decisions on petitions.
in writing. - european horticulture has a huge potential which is not fully exploited, as it faces many obstacles which appropriate legislation at international level can remove or at least minimise. the sector generates close to 1/5 (18%) of the total value of agricultural production in the union, using very little land. with appropriate support, especially from the legal side, it can contribute to enhancing the eu's competitiveness on global markets. horticulture is highly sensitive to weather conditions, which is particularly evident in the context of climate change; in addition, the economic crisis has reduced consumption, reduced the supply of fresh fruit and vegetables and, consequently, reduced investment in the development of the sector. plantation owners are also reluctant to join producer organisations, as a result of the lack of support for such initiatives in the member states. recently, the impact of certain neonicotinoid insecticides on the health of bees and therefore also on plants has also been discussed. we need more, more detailed research and analysis here. investments in training, appropriate study pathways and advisory services will certainly pay dividends in the future, providing skilled workers, while supporting local production and encouraging greater consumption of fruit and vegetables are actions that will benefit both producers and consumers.
in writing. - the report on the future of the european horticultural sector is a noteworthy document, above all because it expresses the european parliament's concern for the horticultural sector, which as such retains its distinctive characteristics against the background of the european agricultural production policy framework. the report contains a number of statements that cannot be substantiated. first, it calls for the current restrictions on the use of certain neonicotinoids, which have recently been banned by the european commission because of their negative effects on bee populations, to be reconsidered. i think it's way too early to go back to this. i am also opposed to the opening up of a wider field for the use of chemical plant protection products beyond the standards laid down in european legislation. while i am opposed to any promotion of gmos in european agriculture and horticulture, i am convinced that the eu needs a bold and comprehensive discussion on gmos, rather than simply avoiding the subject. instead of introducing gmos back door in reports of this kind, we should consider the whole problem in all its aspects and establish uniform rules throughout the eu. in view of the many controversies and shortcomings of the document, i have decided to vote against the report as presented.
in writing. - horticulture is a very important sector, not only because of its significant share in the total value of agricultural production in the eu (18%), but also because of its health and cultural aspects. many europeans pay particular attention to the safety and quality of the products they consume, and they want to be able to buy them as easily as possible. uncertainty in supply chains has led to small producers and breeders refraining from investing or significantly reducing their investments. this has resulted in a decline in production efficiency and global competitiveness. the establishment of appropriate supply chain codes of conduct and the strengthening of the legislative framework in each member state could provide an incentive for producers to develop and become more active. they should be encouraged to innovate, to become more competitive and to be dynamic within the producer organisation. the horticultural sector has much to gain from the use of available genetic technologies. there is also considerable potential for precision farming. producers in the horticultural sector still rarely belong to producer organisations and associations, and tailored incentives to use business support or advice can help them to formulate a plan of action and development so that they can continue to provide healthy and high quality food to europeans while creating their own jobs and livelihoods.
in writing. - one of the first signs of change is, as a report by euromonitor international on the horticulture industry shows, the diversification of distribution channels. the garden producers in eastern europe have chosen it to compensate for possible business failures and to support their image. this also applies to domestic producers, who can now reach both buyers in larger urban agglomerations and customers in the periphery of cities. the diversification of distribution channels, while increasing competition on the market, ensures that garden centres' customers always receive products of the highest quality. this is a way of deterring international diy networks from taking over the market. in most european countries, garden centres have faced a serious challenge. they had to contend with international diy networks with powerful foreign capital. a large proportion of retail gardening establishments have emerged from this confrontation with a strong hand through, among other things, modernisation, expansion, professional service and offering customers a wide range of high quality products.
in writing. - torture is defined in article 1 of the convention on the prohibition of torture as 'any act by which severe pain or suffering, whether physical or mental, is intentionally inflicted on a person for the purpose of obtaining from him or her or a third person information or a confession, of punishing him or her for an act he or she has committed or is suspected of having committed, or of intimidating or coercing him or her or a third person, or for any other purpose arising from any form of discrimination'. freedom from torture is one of the most fundamental human rights. the convention indicates that no exceptional circumstances, such as a state of war, the threat of war, lack of internal political stability or any other exceptional situation, may justify the use of torture. despite the many laws and conventions that have been established, we still encounter inhuman treatment that violates human dignity and personal freedom. and yet, it is taken for granted that freedom from torture is absolute freedom, with no exception to the rule. therefore, this inhuman treatment of human beings deserves to be condemned unequivocally and unanimously as a manifestation of the barbarism of the 21st century.
in writing. - i voted in favor of the report on the eradication of torture in the world (2013/2169(ini)). this report clearly outlines the importance of eradicating torture and the importance of implementing the necessary means to do so. as the report states, the response to the change in the eu guidelines in 2012 should ‘reflect a holistic policy approach, including the promotion of an adequate legislative and judicial framework for the effective prevention and prohibition of torture, monitoring of places of detention, efforts to address impunity, and the full and effective rehabilitation of torture victims, backed up by credible, consistent and coherent action’. furthermore, the eu is and has been the beacon of light in protecting human rights and has abolished the death penalty, and thus we must insist that ‘no exceptions from the absolute prohibition of torture and practices involving cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment can be justified, and that states have an obligation to implement safeguards to prevent the perpetration of torture and ill-treatment, and to ensure accountability and access to effective remedies and reparations at all times’. the eu must continue to protect and promote worldwide the importance of an end to torture both in wars and in times of peace.

vice-president of the commission. - mr president, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr mayer, and the responsible parliamentary committee for dealing with this file so diligently. it is necessary to change the rules we have today for a very simple reason: digital technologies have modified the way we arrange our travel, especially our holidays. in the 1990s, most europeans picked out a prearranged package deal from a brochure and booked it at their local travel agency. today consumers are increasingly booking customised packages online, either from one trader or from several commercially-linked ones. this is why the commission has made a proposal to modernise the existing rules in order to adapt them to market developments and bring them into the digital age. the 1990 package travel directive has given consumers important rights regarding information, liability for the package trip, and protection in case the organiser of the package trip enters insolvency. however, with online bookings of customised combinations, more and more travellers are not protected by the directive, and their protection might be uncertain even if they are. when revising these rules, the commission aims to extend protection for consumers to include both pre-arranged packages and customised combinations – especially those arranged online – which are often referred to as dynamic packages. at the same time, we propose introducing a minimum level of protection in the form of compulsory insolvency protection for linked travel arrangements, which are looser combinations of travel services. these changes will increase protection for almost 120 million trips in the eu per year. this will lead to more transparency and more legal certainty while closing legal loopholes and removing outdated rules. it is not only the consumers who will benefit but businesses too, as the new directive will scrap outdated information requirements, such as the need to reprint brochures. the new directive will also facilitate cross-border transactions through increased harmonisation and mutual recognition of national insolvency protection schemes. it is important to maintain a careful balance between the interests of consumers and the interests of the industry, and between the different types of travel businesses. regarding the level of harmonisation, the commission recognises that parliament has found a very balanced solution. while reducing legal fragmentation, the compromise solution you propose would give member states the possibility – in exceptional cases – to extend the organiser’s liability for the proper performance of a package and the organiser’s obligations to obtain insolvency protection, in accordance with national traditions. while this deviates from the commission proposal, we nonetheless consider that it constitutes a reasonable basis for further negotiations. the commission believes, however, that the proposed definition of linked travel arrangements is too narrow. this category would have virtually no practical relevance, and it therefore requires further examination. overall, though, i would like to say to the rapporteur and to his collaborators that the report he is putting to the vote tomorrow is well-balanced and will bolster protection for consumers. the vote tomorrow will also add momentum to the debate in the council, so the new package rule could become law soon.
rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on transport and tourism. - mr president, on behalf of my committee, i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr mayer, for his good work. the objectives of the committee on transport and tourism (tran) were as follows. first, the new directive should ensure that consumers benefit from a high level of protection when purchasing a combination of travel services. second, at the same time it is necessary to establish a level playing field between market players selling travel packages, remove legal obstacles to cross-border trade and reduce compliance costs for businesses. in conclusion, we welcome the fact that, in spite of a tight timetable, the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, in good cooperation with the tran committee, has achieved the following: a new definition of linked travel arrangements based on a distinction from the travel package; a strengthening of provisions in the pre-contractual information; tighter provision in favour of consumers; more favourable conditions in the event of the contract being terminated; liability for performance of the package; and an increase in accommodation coverage, taking it up to eur[nbsp ]125 per night.
the proposed regulation is part of the programme for climate protection and the fight against climate change. the timetable proposed in the regulation takes into account the very long lead-in period for the withdrawal of all fluorinated gases used in the various appliances we use every day. the long transition period will last until 2022. we will not be phasing out fluorinated gases from refrigeration systems until 2022, and from air conditioners until 2025. so we can see that the adjustment period is relatively long. the regulation also draws attention to the certification system for persons working in services, in services, under which these workers will have the appropriate powers to perform their activities, knowing that these activities must be subject to special controls. in this regard, the security system is much broader. we're also required to recover the fluorinated gases from all the equipment. it's important to be aware that these gases are not getting into the atmosphere. the quota system for producers and importers reduces the amount allocated each year. it's a very good solution. thank you, and i think this is one of the better regulations.

on behalf of the ppe group. freedom of movement for workers is one of the foundations of the european union. it was already enshrined in the founding treaties of the european communities, which shows that it was one of the most important aspects of integration for the founding fathers. despite the fact that european union citizens have been able to enjoy freedom of movement for many years, only 3% of them do, as edit bauer pointed out. this group is predominantly employed, which in turn stimulates economic growth, gives workers better employment opportunities and enables employers to draw on a wider pool of skilled workers. unfortunately, on the one hand, those interested in mobility still face many obstacles, including those related to administrative requirements, inadequate law enforcement, lack of access to information. on the other hand, it is worrying that more than half of eu citizens do not recognise the value of freedom of movement for workers. the shocking fact is that the data also come from member states where there is a huge problem in finding work. this phenomenon should also be seen as a source of low mobility of people within the single market. if half of citizens do not see the positive aspects of finding a job in another member state, then no facilitation will translate into increased mobility. this situation is further exacerbated by the rhetoric of politicians in some member states who see open labour markets as more risks than opportunities and use negative public attitudes to build support for the upcoming elections, even at the expense of the future of the european union. in this context, i see a huge role for the european commission, which should take action to make the freedom of movement and of employment meaningful. many of the proposals in the directive are aimed at improving access to information, advice and support to the relevant institutions to make them more conducive to the mobility of european union citizens. let us remember that europe is still emerging from the crisis and mobility is one of the important sources of economic growth. as politicians, we have a duty to ensure that citizens who want to work freely can do so throughout the european union.
in writing. the free movement of workers is one of the foundations of the eu's functioning, and ensuring that all citizens and their families can make full use of it is therefore of fundamental importance. this principle also entails improving the situation of equal opportunities in the territory of all member states. it should also be borne in mind that the free movement of workers has a major impact on the family lives of millions of workers in the eu. greater choice of country, job and employer itself has a major impact on education and career decisions. for this reason, any discrimination against employees is unacceptable. however, for the free movement of workers system to function as intended, it is necessary to focus not only on the rights and obligations of workers but also on those of employers. both will benefit from the increased effectiveness and uniformity of the applicable laws based on eu legislation and directly affecting the proper functioning of the internal market. the risks and side effects of increased labour mobility, such as brain drain and the outflow of young people abroad, should also be noted. this is a problem that is mainly faced by the less developed countries, but the long-term opportunities that this situation brings must also be emphasised. some of the workers will return to their countries and can become drivers of progress in their regions or fields. these issues should be closely monitored.

in writing. the current political situation in ukraine and the recurring insecurity of gas supplies to europe from russia point to energy policy challenges in the days leading up to the european council. the recent collapse of the world economy, from which we are still trying to recover, has increased uncertainty and highlighted the weaknesses of individual countries in energy security and environmental protection. countries, either alone or in alliances, are reviewing the fundamentals of their energy policies. government programs to stimulate the economies of highly industrialized countries are painted in every possible shade of green. the terms 'green economy' and 'reducing co2 emissions' have become part of the political vocabulary. so what are the key trends in the ever-evolving scenario that will determine the future energy policy of the european union until 2030? energy, the environment and the economy are interconnected. this linkage influences and is shaped by international politics. the common energy policy must be and will be europe's next great integration project, taking into account: • fossil fuels, which will remain crucial for some time to come; • the growing demand for energy, accompanied by the growing need for energy saving and energy efficiency; • the shift of the global economic centre of gravity towards asia, due to china and india, which will have long-term political and energy consequences; • solidarity between member states in the field of energy priorities.

in writing. - the new legislative procedures (delegated and implementing acts) which were implemented after the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon gave more powers to the european parliament, but at the same time forced the adaptation of existing legislation to new methods of law-making. as a result of the conferral of 'delegated powers' on the european commission, it may amend existing documents accepted by the european parliament and inform the other institutions accordingly. however, in the event of objections from the ep, the commission delegated regulation may be rejected. this is the case with the commission proposal to amend regulation (eu) no 1169/2011 of the european parliament and of the council on food information to consumers in the context of the definition of 'engineered nanomaterials'. information on all ingredients present in food produced using nanotechnology must be provided on the packaging so that the consumer is aware of the contents of the product he intends to purchase. nanomaterials are defined by relevant international legislation (i.e. commission recommendation 2011/696/eu) and the aforementioned regulation enables the european commission to adapt these definitions to take account of technical and scientific progress. at the same time, it excludes from the definition of 'engineered nanomaterials' food additives presented in the union lists. the incompatibility of such a derogation with the [nbsp]regulations and with the overriding objective of the legislative measure, namely the protection of consumers' health, leads to the rejection of the commission's proposal.
in writing. - the new act will regulate the rules on food labelling in a comprehensive manner. the most important changes to the current rules concern, among others, the introduction of requirements to improve the legibility of labels, mandatory nutrition information, the display of clear and complete information on allergens, the indication of the country of origin for pork, lamb and goat meat and poultry meat, and other requirements. the new rules are designed to ensure that labels are more legible, making it easier for consumers to find the information they need about food products when they shop. for this reason, the minimum font height for the mandatory information to be displayed on the label has been set, i.e. a 'height x' of at least 1,2 mm, whereas for packaging with a maximum surface area of less than 80 cm2, the minimum 'height x' may be at least 0,9 mm. it is also important that mandatory food information must be indelible and must not be hidden, obscured, reduced or interrupted by other printing or illustration.
in writing. - europe needs to reform its data protection laws. in the age of modern computer technology, more than two decades of legislation cannot ensure adequate protection of europeans' data online. citizens expect a high level of protection of personal data under a single european law. the legislative package adopted by parliament, comprising two instruments, namely the general data protection regulation and the directive on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data for the purpose of crime prevention, addresses concerns about the supervision of data processing and is a major step towards restoring confidence in the digital economy. the main points of the regulatory update, stricter penalties for companies that do not comply with the restrictions, limits on user profiles and stronger and more independent data protection authorities will help to restore that trust by allowing real enforcement from businesses to comply with the rules. under the new rules, only the minimum amount of data needed to provide the service will be collected, data will be protected from being processed by third country governments, and the possibility of data being traded without our knowledge or consent will be severely curtailed. in addition, the new directive introduces major changes to the way information is processed by the police and courts in criminal matters. the european parliament must defend the rights of citizens without depriving law enforcement of the means to fight crime.
in writing. - with the rapid development of modern computer technologies, we should ensure the protection of the processing of personal data for the purposes of crime prevention. with the rapid development of computer technology, the european union needs to keep updating its rules on the protection of personal data within the framework of a single european law. the new rules must improve the effectiveness of law enforcement in the fight against crime, while protecting civil rights.
in writing. - following the scandal generated by the nsa case in america, which also involved the european union in general and some of its member states in particular, the issue of the processing of personal data for the purpose of crime prevention could represent a difficult juncture. the issue of privacy is becoming more and more topical, and we must not forget that the processing of personal data is a sensitive matter. at the same time, crime prevention also passes through the tools that provide for the use of personal data. it is therefore necessary to find a fair compromise which will protect the citizen and at the same time hold the guilty ones accountable.
in writing. - the directive lays down rules relating to the processing of personal data for the purposes of the prevention, prosecution and detection of criminal offences. it also sets out the objectives of protecting the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons, in particular the right to the protection of personal data, while ensuring a high level of public security and ensuring the exchange of personal data between competent authorities in the european union. the scope of the directive is not limited to cross-border data processing but also covers all data processing operations carried out by the competent authorities as defined in the directive. the directive repeals outdated and dysfunctional existing rules and replaces them with a directive introducing enforceable rules that ensure a much higher level of protection of personal data.
the need to handle increasingly heavy air traffic requires a practical approach and proper regulation. unfortunately, not all european countries are committed to the single european sky initiative, which also translates into inconvenience and increased passenger handling costs. the commission notes that the airport services agreement with ryanair was signed on 28 june 2013 and that the agreement was signed on 27 june 2013. with a view to continuing to improve travel conditions, i ask the commission to take appropriate action in cooperation with the member states.
in writing. - launched in 2000, the single european sky initiative (ses) aimed at bringing air traffic management and navigation services under the common transport policy. nevertheless, 14 years later, ses is far from perfect. costs of the fragmentation of european airspace coupled with the anticipated growth in air-traffic, efficiency and use of the european network routes are a few of the reasons why the commission launched a recast of the regulation on ses implementation. the current report supports the commission’s recast and proposes further means to make the proposal more practical – especially with regard to implementation. specifically, the report seeks to include a social dimension in the regulation, to create much-needed indicators covering social, cultural and staffing conditions in the atm sector; it further calls on member states to undertake enhanced cooperation to make ses more inclusive and flexible. lastly, the report vetoes initial plans to oblige member states to separate and liberalise support services from the core services. the social and organisational cost would be unpredictable and the benefits for aviation questionable. coping with passenger demand for delay-free, environmentally-friendly and affordable air travel requires a change in the current system. this report is important in achieving this goal, therefore i voted to support it.
in writing. - the idea of creating a single european sky (ses) has brought together air traffic management and air navigation services within the eu's common transport policy. this is a highly complex process, the main objective of which should be to deliver tangible benefits to the european air traffic management industry, airspace users, airlines and passengers. it should not be forgotten that the safety of european citizens is a key factor in optimising and speeding up the functioning of european airspace. they must also not be exposed to unjustified costs related to the implementation of the ses.
in writing. - the single european sky policy is largely on paper, as the european commission says. therefore, it is necessary to make the aviation sector supervisors and air navigation organisations independent of the state authorities and other entities. in its reference to other bodies and organisations, the communication merely indicates the direction of future legislative changes. in particular, the commission provides that the members of the so-called 'performance review body' whose functions are performed by eurocontrol should be elected directly by the commission and not by the representatives of the member states. at the same time, the communication provides for the extension of eurocontrol's competence in its function as air traffic management network manager to include certain aspects of airspace design. the simplified management structures are also intended to improve the functioning of the organisation.
the increasing use of the internet in commercial transactions makes it necessary to guarantee the quality of the services offered by the tourism sector as well. therefore, a focused approach to harmonisation in the area of consumer rights, in this case travellers, is of the utmost importance. in practice, this translates into, among other things, issues of correct information about the service offered or the consumer's right to terminate the contract in the event of the operator's failure to fulfil its obligation. this is essential in the face of the regularly recurring cases of insolvency of professional suppliers resulting in non-performance of the contract and the frequent practice of leaving customers to their own devices. the provisions of the directive impose an obligation to organise return travel in such a situation.
in writing. - the sale of tourist services and events via the internet has increased rapidly in recent years, so it is necessary to update the regulations. it is important that the rules are balanced and take into account the interests of both tourism companies and consumers. for example, information obligations on the part of the tour operator should be strengthened, but this should not result in an excessive burden. the rules also cover situations where the price of a journey changes. in certain circumstances, the traveller must be able to withdraw from the contract without suffering financial loss or the right to participate in a tourist event of the same value. organisers should also be obliged to provide immediate assistance if a traveller is in trouble during the journey for which the organiser is not responsible. of course, such assistance cannot be a financial burden for the organiser, since it had no influence on the situation of the traveller. it may also happen that the tour operator becomes insolvent and[nbsp]there is a need for comprehensive protection. this is not only financial security but also direct transport with return in the event that the traveller is 'displaced' in a member state other than his country of origin. the adopted report is parliament's position and a good starting point for further work to ensure greater legal certainty for travellers without imposing too much on businesses.
in writing. - the obligations arising from the directive will cover a greater number of companies, which will equalise their chances in organising tourist events. this will also increase consumer safety, as more operators will have to provide certain guarantees in the event of the inability to provide a service or its poor performance, says krzysztof piątek from the polish association of tour operators. the draft also envisages the inclusion of sellers of arranged tourist services, i.e. those where the trader refers to offers from other companies that can be used as part of a single trip. when a consumer chooses such services, he concludes separate contracts with different sellers. an organised tourist service differs from a package tourism in that it does not include the essential elements of the latter, such as the total or all-inclusive price. the draft directive requires retailers who facilitate the purchase of 'arranged tourist services' to clearly explain to travellers that the organiser of the tourist service is solely responsible for the provision of the service, explains przemysław kral, a lawyer at przemysław kral law firm. this means that the trader is only responsible for his own offer. in the case of a traditional tourist event, the seller is responsible for all the services that are part of the tourist event. travellers will, however, be able to direct their complaints or claims also through the retailer and the travel agency where they purchased the trip in question, "kral's lawyer said.
in writing. - the european parliament very rarely deals with tourism services, which is a fast-growing sector. the response to the changes in tourism therefore seems to be delayed. in recent years, the changes have mainly been the introduction of online commerce, whereby the consumer selects offers and makes his own travel and stay plans online. in other words, consumers are increasingly reluctant to use a ready-made and comprehensive package of tourist services in favour of choosing individual transport or hotel services. these increasingly visible changes cannot relieve operators selling individual tourism services from providing decent minimum service standards. these basic requirements are the reliable information of tourists about the products and the obligation for operators to provide security for various emergency situations, such as the need to return the deposits collected if the service is not provided or the obligation to ensure that travellers return home in the event of the tourist office's insolvency. in my view, such legal and financial requirements should in any event apply to carriers, which would save many tourists from the problems they may encounter during their travel or stay.
in writing. - finding alternatives to most of the substances currently depleting the ozone layer and strengthening competitiveness in the field of innovative refrigeration, air-conditioning and heating technologies are among the priorities of the european union. according to previous eu guidelines, protecting and preventing further environmental degradation by reducing greenhouse gas emissions requires reducing current emissions by up to 95% by 2050. and in less than 16 years, by 2030, the reduction must be as much as 72-73%. during the preparation of the commission proposal, the need to introduce equipment using alternative technologies in such a way as to encourage investment and innovation, in particular by small and medium-sized enterprises, was identified to rely on alternative equipment with a high penetration rate from the start of their operations. the proposal to introduce a system of producer responsibility for the recovery, recycling, recovery or destruction of fluorinated greenhouse gases is noteworthy. an effective system of accountability is necessary for the implementation of reforms and such changes should be welcomed. i support this report because i see the need to start implementing the conclusions as soon as possible. the current state of greenhouse gas emissions requires immediate reduction actions and i hope that the finally agreed text will allow the intended short and long-term targets to be effectively achieved.
in writing. - fluorinated greenhouse gases are a group of chemicals that contain fluorine. f-gases have specific properties that make them useful agents in a wide range of applications. although these gases are present in very low concentrations in the atmosphere, their emissions are similar to those of greenhouse gases and contribute 14% to the current warming trend. all greenhouse gases are related to human activity. the european union has adopted measures to regulate emissions of certain greenhouse gases under its obligations under the kyoto protocol. the european commission's main objective is to reduce their volume and thus contribute to the reduction of fluorinated gas emissions. to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, the eu has set up a market trading system, with specific rules for fluorinated greenhouse gases.
in writing. - the free movement of workers is the basis for a well-functioning internal market in the eu, enshrined in article 45 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union. unfortunately, many workers, employers and officials still lack sufficient knowledge of the legislation in force in this area. the free movement of workers is a key condition for the development of the eu labour market, especially now that we are facing the consequences of the economic crisis. it is estimated that while we are struggling with recent record unemployment in the eu, almost 1.7 million jobs are unfilled. it is therefore essential to facilitate the exercise of the rights of permanent, seasonal and frontier workers whose place of employment and residence are in two different member states, and of persons engaged in an economic activity for the purpose of providing services. discrimination on grounds of nationality or residence in respect of employment, remuneration, tax and social rights is also unacceptable. therefore, legislation is needed to ensure that workers are adequately protected in all eu countries.
in writing. - current legislation covers projects with a production capacity of at least 500[nbsp]000 cubic metres of gas per day. many shale gas projects have much lower production thresholds due to the environmentally unfavourable nature of the fracking process. it is also a water-intensive technology, and poland is water-poor. environmental impact assessment should therefore be mandatory for all projects related to the extraction and exploration of unconventional hydrocarbons (shale gas and oil, coalbed methane, etc.), irrespective of the size of the production, including shale gas projects where hydraulic fracturing technology is used. the environmental impact assessment (eia) directive covers a wide range of public and private projects. it sets out the basic criteria for the project, including the information that must be submitted to the national authorities for final approval. unfortunately, the previous amendments were dropped: aimed at deleting the provisions related to the environmental analysis at the exploration stage, concerning the environmental assessment only for extraction above 500[nbsp ]000 cubic metres. however, i voted in favour of the report because i believe that its adoption will not lead to the blocking of exploration for unconventional gas in poland. moreover, the directive does not enter into force immediately, as do regulations and decisions, so there is no cause for alarm at this stage.
in writing. - the protection of the environment is one of the fundamental duties of every citizen of the european union, regardless of his or her profession or material status. how we treat the environment now will determine the world in which future generations will live. the ideal is a 'green economy' with sustainable projects that are developed in terms of their impact on resource efficiency, climate change and biodiversity loss. unfortunately, like any ideal, it is currently unattainable. the authors of this document therefore seek to address current issues and challenges. the idea is to provide the european union with the efficient tool needed to rationally assess and control the impact of new public and private projects. the updating of the current legislation is necessary because the global economy is constantly evolving and new issues requiring regulation, such as potential extraction and[nbsp]use of shale gas, will be increasingly emerging in the near future. however, it should be borne in mind that not all national economies are at a similar level of development and that the harmonisation of rules across the eu will create problems for those countries whose economies are based on older technologies. at the same time, new legislation can provide an additional incentive to stimulate the development of new ventures, but it should be stressed that this is a long-term process.
in writing. - the discovery of unconventional energy hydrocarbon deposits, such as shale gas, in selected eu countries and the emergence of economic methods of extracting them have created the need for comprehensive regulation of this issue. the aim is to strike a delicate balance between ensuring high environmental standards and reducing the level of risk incurred by private operators exploring and subsequently exploiting unconventional hydrocarbon deposits. i support the report as it meets my expectations in this respect. it provides an incentive for investors by avoiding the need to carry out a complex environmental impact assessment for each well, which would only hinder the potential benefits that shale gas can bring to europe. on the other hand, any operator exploring for oil reserves must make every effort to ensure that the environment is not harmed by the exploration for hydrocarbons for energy. i nevertheless insist that any decision to start the industrial exploitation of the reservoir be preceded by an environmental impact assessment and be made in accordance with the most far-reaching conservation measures. moreover, i take this opportunity to once again appeal to the polish government to fulfil its obligation to adopt the renewable energy sources act. the commission considers that the measures in question constitute state aid within the meaning of article 107 (1) of the treaty.
in writing. - environmental impact assessment (eia) is a process that ensures that environmental impacts are taken into account before decisions are made on the development of a site or the implementation of a project. the basic requirements for environmental impact assessments are laid down in the environmental impact assessment directive.
in writing. - these provisions require the member states of the european union to collect and transmit to the statistical office of the european commission, eurostat, statistical data on trade between them. these provisions do not specify which institutions in each member state are to be responsible for implementing this obligation, leaving the organisation of the operation of intrastat to the discretion of the individual countries. in the european union countries, there is a system of data collection which consists of the submission of reports by economic operators to the designated institutions or offices on a monthly cycle. it is recommended that international trade in goods statistics should record all goods that add or subtract from a country's material resources, i.e. goods brought into or taken out of the country.

in writing. - of the 500 million european citizens, only a small percentage seems to know and exercise their rights as union citizens. this notion was stressed in the spring 2013 eurobarometer, which revealed that 53% of europeans feel they do not know their rights as eu citizens. to enhance awareness and knowledge to the rights and responsibilities of eu citizenship, the commission added to its 2013 eu citizenship report 12 new actions in six key areas. the corresponding ep report builds on these areas, while adding several elements to the commission’s proposal: the report stresses that citizens must have access to all the necessary information to enable them to practise fully their economic, social, administrative, legal and cultural rights. it further calls on national, regional and local authorities to promote understanding of eu citizenship and explain the benefits to individuals. moreover, it encourages member states to give more space to political education on eu affairs in their school curricula. lastly, the report calls on the eu institutions to improve transparency and access to public documents. with that, the adopted report will help promote active eu citizenship and the effective application of citizens’ rights in everyday matters across the eu. therefore i voted to support this report.

in writing. - the hong kong international convention for safe and environmentally sound recycling (hkc) was adopted on 15 may 2009 under the auspices of the international maritime organisation. the convention covers the design, construction, maintenance and preparation of ships in such a way as to facilitate their safe and environmentally sound recycling, without prejudice to safety and operational efficiency. it also covers the principles for the safe and environmentally sound operation of ship recycling facilities and establishes appropriate mechanisms for the enforcement of proper ship recycling. on 20 november 2013, the parliament and the council adopted a new regulation on ship recycling. it aims to ensure the environmentally friendly recycling of ships in the eu, in particular by excluding their dismantling in countries with environmentally harmful dismantling practices. global action is needed to achieve safer and more environmentally friendly ship recycling standards in the eu and it is therefore necessary to ensure the swift ratification of the hong kong convention.
in writing. - the convention was adopted at an international conference held in hong kong in may 2009. the international agreement, drawn up with the significant involvement of the imo, was intended to be a further step towards ensuring safe, environmentally friendly ship scrapping, especially in the light of the ineffectiveness of the existing rules in this area. however, the convention has not yet entered into force, as the number of states that must accept it (by ratification or accession) to enter into force has been set at a relatively high level.
in writing. - the economic and financial crisis has affected many eu countries, but not all have been affected to the same extent. in particular, fiscal balance has been disturbed in greece, portugal, ireland and cyprus, and it is important that these countries have received the necessary assistance. in these countries, measures were taken to reduce the deficit, which was to encourage business investment and to eliminate the dualism of the labour market. however, the drastic reduction in social spending imposed on these countries as part of their economic adjustment programmes has in many cases contributed to a worsening of the social situation. many of the expectations associated with these actions have not been met, which requires a re-examination of the likelihood of the long-term projections being realised. jobs have also declined and conditions have worsened. the expected increase in employment has not come on time, as we are only now seeing a slight recovery, which has led to a drastic destabilisation of social security systems. the situation was also exacerbated by public and private sector spending cuts and the lack of an effective system to combat tax fraud. we must remember that the problem of widespread poverty and social exclusion is much more difficult to treat than to prevent. an active employment policy, the repair of the credit system and the establishment of crisis management mechanisms are necessary. social exclusion must be tackled decisively and the long-term unemployed must be given the opportunity to return to the labour market.

mr. chairman, please! in order to fully exploit the potential for increased competitiveness and employment offered by the digital single market, the role of telecommunications in all sectors of the economy needs to be enhanced. after three itre regulations in six years, we have finally changed the retail roaming charges for voice, sms and data. the obligation for operators should enter into force in 2016. the main achievement of this regulation is to ensure that the internet remains open. in other words, users have the ability to access and distribute information or use any application of their choice. in addition, for the first time, the regulation includes a definition of net neutrality, which states that net neutrality on the open internet means that traffic should be treated equally. the agreed text also strikes a balance between open access to the internet, where transparency and non-discrimination are ensured, and thus allows the market to continue to develop new innovative products such as specialised services. the proposed regulation also guarantees that specialised services will not in any way harm the open internet, and at the same time the proposed solutions do not allow for the concealment or imposition of additional fees for specialised services. furthermore, internet service providers must not have a detrimental effect on the quality of the existing service.

in writing. global warming is one of the greatest challenges facing developed countries and can only be tackled through concrete international action. aviation is responsible for about 3% of total greenhouse gas emissions, and these levels are rising rapidly. the international civil aviation organisation (icao) estimates that this level has practically doubled between 1990 and 2006. in addition, the lack of concrete action on this issue will cause it to increase to 1900 mt by 2040. the commission's proposal to include aviation in the eu ets, covering all flights that take off from or land in europe, was a fair, temporary solution to this problem. although this assumption was strongly criticised by third countries, the judgment of the european court of justice in the case brought by american airlines showed that this was fully in line with international law. however, this does not change the fact that it will be necessary to find a global agreement at icao level on this matter and to develop an international system of market measures in the coming years. in this context, the european commission should engage in talks with third countries promoting accession to the emissions trading scheme in the years leading up to the global agreement. in addition, other actions will also be important, in particular the establishment of a single european airspace, which would reduce delays and discrepancies in air traffic control.
member of the commission. - mr president, on behalf of my colleague, michel barnier, who cannot be here tonight as he has to attend the informal ecofin council meeting in athens, i would like to congratulate parliament on the swift progress that has been made in recent months on both proposals in this payment package, part of the single market act ii. your support for the commission’s proposals shows that you share the ambition of the commission to achieve a well-functioning payment market. this efficiency consists of finding the optimal balance between innovation, fair competition, secure payments and consumer protection. efficient and secure payments are important for social inclusion but also for the promotion of growth and jobs. let me now briefly turn to the two texts – first of all, the revised directive on payment services (psd2). this will integrate in the same legal framework traditional market players and certain new providers of online payment services. the latter, the so-called third-party payment service providers (tpps), offer consumers the possibility to pay for their online purchase by means of simple electronic credit transfers. this is a good example of innovative payment solutions which are good for consumers and companies. the inclusion of tpps in the scope of the existing directive will ensure that all payment providers are subject to adequate regulation and supervision and ensure competition on equal terms between different actors providing payment solutions. the commission has noted with interest your proposal to provide a mandate to the european banking authority for the development of a single interface for the communication between tpps and other payment service providers. this approach would address the security concerns that have been raised by certain banks. it would also ensure a safer level playing field between the different market players. the commission also welcomes the fact that the committee on economic and monetary affairs (econ) supports the extension of the scope of the directive in different areas, for example by extending the scope to so-called one-leg transactions, meaning that only one part of the transaction has to take place in the european union in order for the directive to apply. this will in particular benefit all those citizens who use money remittance services to send money to their home country outside the eu. i also share the view of econ that it may be useful to review the details of this extension after a certain period of time. with regard to interchange fees for card-based payments, i am happy to note that the econ report broadly supports the proposed regulation. the commission has been working on this proposal for a long time. whilst some operators have criticised it, the proposal was particularly welcomed by consumers and retailers. in addition, the proposal provides the necessary legal certainty which some market operators have been asking for. we hope that clear rules on interchange fees will also encourage new market entrants in the eu card market, which remains dominated by very few actors. finally, we believe that this proposal will encourage innovation around electronic card-payments. this is an important contribution to the digital agenda and europe 2020. the majority of the amendments proposed by econ will clarify and strengthen the impact of the initial proposal. one of the shadow rapporteurs, mr terho, proposes that the rules on interchange fees should apply only to cross-border transactions. this would not be effective. we are trying to create a true internal market where there is no difference between a national and a cross-border transaction. with regard to debit cards, the introduction of an additional absolute ceiling of 7 eurocents per transaction – above the initial cap of 0.2[nbsp ]% of the transaction amount for debit card transactions – goes further than our proposal. as the lower of the two amounts will apply, the interchange fee for transactions of more than eur[nbsp ]35 will be no higher than 7 eurocents. merchants and consumers will benefit from this approach, which will contribute to encouraging the development of large-scale electronic payments. the commission would therefore be open to revising its opinion. the econ report also proposes extending caps from consumer cards to commercial cards and to some cards issued by three-party schemes. the commission’s proposal focused on consumer cards only. we believe that commercial cards and three-party scheme cards are of much more limited use. thus, we are not convinced that the same type of legal caps should be extended to these cards as well. however, we are willing to consider this further. in any event, this is a matter that we will continue to look at during the legislative process. to conclude, the commission welcomes the progress made on these important files. we hope that similar progress will be made in the council in the near future, so that both legislators can work towards a speedy adoption of this package, to the benefit of consumers, merchants and the economy at large.

in writing. - it is perhaps surprising that after so many years of the european social fund, neither the member states nor the european commission have developed mechanisms to evaluate the effectiveness of european funds spent on the activation of older people and activities related to active ageing. in an age of aging societies, of challenging labour markets, of technological advances, we cannot afford to ignore the potential that older people have. as a member of the committee on employment and social affairs, i was the author of the opinion on the report by mr balcytis, and i would like to express my strong support for the conclusions and recommendations contained in the final document prepared by the committee on budgetary control, which i supported in the vote. and we talk about the need to constantly learn new skills, to keep up with technology and the increasingly computerized world. people my age need training and help to stay in the job market. more and more member states are introducing pension reforms aimed at extending working life. in this respect, we can achieve greater results with the european social fund, but to improve the efficiency of the use of funds, we must first create mechanisms to evaluate the instruments currently in use.
in writing. - the arrest and subsequent death in custody of sergei magnitsky cast real doubts on the independence and impartiality of the judicial institutions in russia. not only was sergei magnitsky imprisoned without a trial but, according to reports by two independent investigations, he was subjected to inhumane prison conditions, deliberate neglect and torture, which probably resulted in his death. being a member of several international organisations, russia has committed itself to protecting and promoting human rights, fundamental freedoms and the rule of law. unfortunately the specific case of sergei magnitsky, among other cases, highlights many shortcomings in respect for the rule of law in the country and its implementation. russia is an important strategic partner for the eu, that fact is indisputable. nevertheless, the eu has a responsibility to uphold and foster values of human rights and democracy. i therefore support the recommendations in the current report, asking for the establishment of a common european list of russian officials believed to have been involved in the death of sergei magnitsky. i support the proposal, following on from that, to ban these officials from entering the eu and bar them from benefiting from any financial assets they or their immediate family might hold within the eu.
in writing. - the new digital and online media platforms have increased the diversity, pluralism and accessibility of information, allowing it to reach out to people, including in countries where the freedom of the press is restricted. this trend can be employed for the promotion of democratic values, media freedom and human rights around the world. moreover, it can be used as a means to communicate eu policies, shape european perspectives and provide the audience with reliable information. in line with this understanding, the current report proposes to make use of european broadcasting media to achieve these objectives. particularly, the report advocates establishing a coherent and robust eu media broadcasting strategy in the context of the eu’s external relations that will: provide a platform for exchange of opinions and debates; support media independence; and help train future leading journalists in the eu and beyond. equally important, the report asks to define and organise the public service broadcasting remit to develop an independent and professional broadcasting media environment in third countries too. these recommendations are important for the advancement of professional and objective broadcasting media in the eu and across the world, therefore i voted to support the report.
in writing. - i have voted in support of the council’s position at first reading with a view to the adoption of a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the sound level of motor vehicles and of replacement silencing systems, and amending directive 2007/46/ec and repealing directive 70/157/eec (17695/1/2013 – c7-0060/2014 – 2011/0409(cod)). this regulation will help the environment by limiting air and noise pollution levels. it will be implemented on all vehicles in three phases with the first starting on 1 january 2017, which will, for example, result in a reduction to a 68db limit value for passenger cars. as was the concern of many of my colleagues and myself, we have insisted on and got approved protection for the blind and other vulnerable people through the installation of appropriate vehicle alerting systems in electric vehicles. also, the parliament and council have agreed that such systems should be mandatory; it has been agreed that this will apply to new vehicle types within three years following the date of application of the regulation and within five years for all electric and hybrid electric vehicles.
in writing. - the european union needs effective instruments and a solid legislative foundation to strengthen its ability to enforce its trade rights. the union is currently suffering from a lack of an adequate horizontal legal framework to provide the tools to defend compliance with wto and other international agreements. the adoption of the relevant rules will not only broaden the scope of the action, but also make it possible to enter new markets more safely. the eu has only resorted to retaliation on a few occasions in the past few years, but the problem is also the timing of the response. currently, in the absence of a suitable horizontal legal framework, decisions are adopted under the ordinary legislative procedure, which takes between 15 and 31 months. the scope and the proposed remedies should be carefully considered, but speed should also be considered. the sooner the eu receives this instrument, the sooner it will be possible to start a more efficient trade policy. the union should also have at its disposal certain means to enable it to pursue activities related to the service sector. even now, there are trade disputes in which the eu could consider applying remedies in this sector. it should be borne in mind that the rail sector is one of the key and fast-growing sectors of the economy and its inclusion in the area of union competence in question would have a positive impact on the union's credibility by enabling it to enforce its rights efficiently.
in writing. - actions to promote and achieve development will be an area of particular interest to the european union in 2015. this does not, of course, mean that the development before and after 2015 is underestimated, as action to promote it is continuously present through many forms of union action. the various actors involved in development should alert the public to the fact that one in five europeans is suffering from poverty. the year 2015 should be an opportunity to renew a sense of solidarity between people, where it is not about where you live or what colour you are, but about the challenges facing families and communities. it is not possible to solve all the problems of disparities in development once and for all with a single decision or programme, but this objective must be constantly borne in mind when implementing different types of action. ngos and youth organisations play a significant role in improving people's living conditions and in strengthening development cooperation. the use of their motivation, creativity and real potential to make a positive difference should be given special consideration when deciding on the allocation of available resources.
in writing. - ensuring the safety of the food supply chain is a delicate and precise task. when it is proposed to replace the many legal bases relating to it with new, uniform financial rules which would be in line with the new multiannual financial framework and the lisbon treaty, particular care and precision are required. nevertheless, the objective of rationalising overly complex and diffuse rules will be an obvious facilitation and improvement. a uniform and simplified financial framework will be of great help in the planning and management of activities related to the food supply chain, the area of crop production, animal health and welfare, plants and plant reproductive material. after all, more effective programming and implementation often directly translates into food chain safety. this regulation should contribute to a better protection of the level of human, animal and plant health throughout the food chain. the extent to which this objective is achieved will also depend on the level of preparation of the national authorities in the field. however, the training programme to which they are subject should also be extended to private sector operators, in view of the benefits of disseminating that information and promoting uniform standards to ensure consumer protection. the introduction of possibilities to support union reference laboratories and projects aimed at improving the efficiency and effectiveness of official controls could also be beneficial.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the proposal for a council directive amending directive 2009/71/euratom establishing a community framework for the nuclear safety of nuclear installations (com(2013)0715 – c7-0385/2013 – 2013/0340(nle)). i feel strongly that nuclear power is a vital and important tool for the production of energy and feel just as strong about using it safely and efficiently. thus, i share the opinion of the rapporteur in that ‘the prevention of incidents and accidents as well as an efficient response in case that an incident or accident do occur. accident preparedness and coordination in case of an accident should be at the very core of nuclear safetyʼ. following the accident at fukushima, the eu carried out stress tests on all nuclear power plants resulting in all of them being deemed safe. to continue this pattern, and more importantly improve even further upon safety standards, it is vital to combine technical improvements with wider safety issues such as governance, transparency and on-site preparedness and response. we should not however underestimate the value that nuclear power brings but by the same token we cannot forget that nuclear power can be dangerous; thus this directive provides for all safety concerns.
in writing. - the stockholm programme sets out the european union's priorities for 2010-14 and aims to meet future challenges and further strengthen the area of justice, freedom and security through concrete actions targeting the needs of citizens. the lisbon treaty and the legally binding eu charter of fundamental rights provide a solid constitutional basis for achieving these objectives. however, some of the areas covered by the programme require additional efforts, especially in terms of law enforcement. in addition, the commission should develop mechanisms to monitor the proper implementation of the justice, freedom and security (jfs) procedures. all binding union objectives must be based on an interinstitutional agreement, as provided for in article 17 of the treaty on european union. it will therefore be necessary to introduce greater transparency so that the european parliament is properly informed at all stages during the conclusion of international agreements. the stockholm programme calls for the development of an internal security strategy for the eu to enhance the protection of citizens and to combat organised crime and terrorism more effectively. in this context, it is necessary to strengthen border controls to counter illegal immigration and cross-border crime while ensuring access for persons in need of protection and vulnerable groups. in conclusion, the union should promote the highest level of protection of human rights and respect for fundamental civil liberties. the consistent implementation of the stockholm programme must reflect the needs of citizens for equal opportunities and gender equality.
in writing. - advanced international coordination is a key issue for the effectiveness of the actions expressed in the agreements on the area of freedom, security and justice. consistency between internal and external human rights policies will also be necessary in the context of fundamental rights. in order to achieve the desired effect, the effective functioning of monitoring mechanisms is necessary, which will ensure public oversight of the strategies implemented on an ongoing basis. the assistance of third countries is also important, but it is important to ensure that the information is obtained in a fully legal and humanitarian manner. it is unacceptable for the union institutions to turn a blind eye to the manifestations of a breach of the space of freedom of nationals of a given state, especially in the context of the implementation of union agreements with third countries. for this reason, the eu should not sign agreements on an area of freedom, security and justice with countries where there is little chance of compliance. the identification by the european commission of areas vulnerable to corruption in the member states will, on the other hand, make it possible to combat corruption more effectively and strengthen the foundations for the development of a society with high standards of transparency and integrity. corruption not only affects the economy by hindering its development and preventing healthy competitive behaviour, but also has a negative impact on human rights. this is of course true both for member states and for third countries.

in writing. the proposed consumer product safety regulation is so important that surveys show that as many as 27% of europeans consider a significant number of products on the market to be unsafe. we will certainly have to work further on the controversial article 7 of the made in mark in the legislative process. the idea of introducing this labelling is a good one, but the most important thing is to implement the law. our priority should be to provide consumers with clear and reliable information not only about the country of origin of a product, but also about whether the product is safe and tested. very often it is not so much the country of origin as the manufacturer. i'm concerned that the way to identify a country as "made in" is quite complicated. we therefore need to give consumers reliable and clear information about how we define country of origin. often a product is the result of a production process in several countries and the 'made in' label is then decided by the 'last significant economically justifiable working or processing' principle. the consumer must be aware of this. as production standards in eu countries are quite similar due to eu legislation, it is a good idea to allow the use of the 'made in eu' mark. sometimes information about a specific place of production can be relevant for consumer behaviour because of persistent stereotypes about certain member states.

in writing. - the adopted report on the amended proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council laying down a procedure for the provision of information in the field of technical regulations and of rules on information society services was intended to harmonise the acts contained in the original directive. one of the most important tasks in the implementation of the single market is to prevent the adoption of national technical regulations and standards which could create additional barriers to trade. in this context, the main assumption of the original directive was that member states would agree to consult the european commission and other countries on new legislative proposals before their potential adoption. over time, the legislative review procedure was gradually extended to all draft technical regulations and standards on industrial, agricultural and fishery products, allowing the free movement of goods. information society services were also included in the procedure due to the need to create a monitoring mechanism for this dynamically developing area. however, member states have retained a large degree of possible freedom to prevent obstacles to technological development in this sector. the harmonisation of the acts contained in the directive will further advance the achievement of the existing procedure, which has contributed both to streamlining national legislation and to identifying the areas of law where harmonisation is necessary.
in writing. - each national standardisation body shall notify the commission and the other european and national standardisation bodies referred to in the annexes to this directive of its draft standards or of amendments to existing standards. the commission may also require the submission of national standardisation programmes, which will then be made available to other member states.
in writing. - the ata carnets department deals with issues related to the functioning of the international customs document, the ata carnet, and the tasks arising from the national chamber of commerce's function as a guaranteeing association in the ata system. the ata carnet department is responsible, among other things, for the correct issuance of ata carnets, the provision of all kinds of information on the operation of the system in poland and worldwide, the ongoing cooperation with the international chamber of commerce in paris, the polish customs administration, polish customs offices and chambers of commerce in 71 countries acting as national guaranteeing associations. the ata carnet is a special international customs document which enables and facilitates the temporary clearance of goods exported for acquisition and exhibition purposes, as well as professional equipment. the ata carnet eliminates the complex customs procedure associated with temporary release. the cardholder does not have to complete the sad, customs declarations or deposits at all borders crossed. this document was prepared by the customs cooperation council with the assistance of the international chambers of commerce office of the international chamber of commerce in paris.

in writing. - under the 'shift2rail' initiative, the european commission will more than triple its spending on rail research and innovation to €450 million between 2014 and 2020, compared with €155 million in the previous period. the budget will be supplemented by a further eur 470 million from the railway sector. the main objectives of the 'shift2rail' set by the commission are: reducing the total life cycle costs of rail transport (i.e. the costs of construction, operation, maintenance and repair of infrastructure and rolling stock) by up to 50%; increasing the total processing capacity by up to 100%; generally increasing the reliability of the services; improving up to 50% depending on the rail market segment.
in writing. - the egf aims to help workers who have lost their jobs as a result of changes in the pattern of world trade to find new employment as quickly as possible. the fund, set up by the european union in 2007, will have a budget of up to 500 million per year. the egf may finance actions under an active labour market policy focusing entirely on the provision of assistance to workers made redundant as a result of globalisation, for example through: job search assistance, career guidance, personalised training and retraining, including it skills and the certification of experience gained, assistance for supervised dismissals and promotion of entrepreneurship or self-employment, specific time-limited measures such as job-search allowances, relocation allowances or allowances for persons undertaking training courses and training, motivation measures, in particular for disadvantaged or older workers, to enable them to stay on the labour market or to re-enter the labour market. applications for funding shall be submitted by the member states. individuals or companies facing job losses and wishing to benefit from the support offered by the fund should contact the relevant national authorities.
in writing. - the deposit guarantee schemes framework is one of the three pillars of the banking union. the goal of this legislative proposal is to safeguard deposits under eur[nbsp ]100 000 in eu countries by a solid ex-ante funding for national funds, financed by banks and not by taxpayers. the text, which forms the compromise of the negotiations between the ep and the council, contains several important elements: (1) deposit guarantee schemes to guarantee deposits under eur[nbsp ]100[nbsp ]000 should reach 0.8[nbsp ]% of covered deposits in 10 years. they should be funded by 70[nbsp ]% of contributions in cash and banks’ contributions should be defined according to the risk profile of banks. (2) payment deadlines will be cut from 20 working days to 7, with a transitional period up to 2024. (3) contributions to the deposit guarantee scheme will be based on the level of the covered deposits and the level of risk of the member institution concerned. (4) depositors will receive clear information on the amount covered, the corresponding guarantee scheme, how to contact it, and all relevant information in the event of insolvency. these elements of the proposal are of high importance in protecting taxpayers and stabilising the eu’s financial system; for these reasons i voted in favour of the text.
