in writing. - under the current legal regime, which is set out in the ucits iv directive, all assets of a ucits fund must be placed in the custody of a depositary. the depositary shall be liable for losses incurred as a result of failure to perform his duties, although both the full limits of this liability and the detailed scope of the duties have been specified by the legal systems of the member states. this type of regulation leaves dangerously wide scope for divergent interpretations of the provisions of the directive by national law and leads to a situation where ucits investors face unequal levels of protection across different jurisdictions. the question of the depositary's liability arises where the custody of the assets of the ucits is entrusted to a sub-depositary and gives rise to undue difficulties of interpretation. the current system of sanctions also shows considerable divergences. moreover, the current remuneration policy contributes to short-term decision-making and encourages excessive risk-taking.

in writing. - the report adopted today concerns the second part of the legislative procedure amending the statute of the court of justice of the eu as regards the number of judges. in recent years, the number of new cases entering the courts has been steadily increasing and exceeding the number of cases decided. the only exception was in 2012, when the number of pending cases was 617 and the number of cases decided was 688. the data clearly show that the court is no longer able to cope with the workload of the accession of new member states and the increase in the number of admissible types of action. the need to increase the number of judges in the court is therefore an unquestionable issue. according to the court of justice, the current number of judges should be supplemented by a further 12, which seems to be the right solution. the union's contribution to the budget of the european schools for the period 2014-2020 is estimated at eur 5 million. each additional judge post, together with administrative costs, represents an expenditure of around eur 1 million per year. the final number of judges is not the most important thing. the issue in this context was the manner in which they were to be recruited, given that not all member states would be able to appoint more than one judge. in this context, i agree with the rapporteur that the best way to solve this problem is to select new judges on the basis of their professional qualifications, rather than their country of origin, where each member state will be able to propose its candidates.
in writing. - the court was set up to support the court of justice and to provide citizens with better legal protection. since the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, it has been the judicial organ of the court of justice of the eu. it was formerly known as the court of first instance. the court of first instance is composed of at least one judge from each member state, currently 27. unlike the court of justice, the court does not have permanent advocates-general. the court of justice shall sit in chambers of five or three judges and, in certain cases, in a single judge. it may also sit as a grand chamber (thirteen judges) or as a full court, where the degree of legal complexity or the weight of the case so requires. in the vast majority (over 80%) of cases brought before the court, the court rules in a formation of three judges.

madam president! the free movement of workers is a consequence of the free movement of persons, which is one of the main foundations of the european union. the promotion and facilitation of the cross-border mobility of workers in the context of their retention of their entitlement to supplementary pensions should be ensured, at least to a minimum extent, by uniform arrangements throughout the community. workers who fear losing their entitlement to supplementary pensions in their new country of residence may refuse to change their place of work. these are, of course, rights which do not fall within the scope of the social protection guaranteed by the social security systems of the member states but which result, for example, from additional agreements concluded in the framework of an employment contract between an employer and an employee. the absence of such regulations may have the effect of restricting the free movement of workers. it is therefore essential to lay down minimum requirements governing the rules for the transfer of supplementary pension rights in order to facilitate cross-border mobility of workers. when we introduce mechanisms to facilitate the change of residence, whether for purely personal reasons or because of the greater possibility of finding work in the country where a person intends to settle, we must aim to ensure that the rights acquired previously are guaranteed in a certain and inviolable way. there are no standards which would give them the chance of being recognised on similar terms in different member states. it is therefore necessary to seek solutions that can be applied throughout the european union, so that the lack of such solutions does not constitute a reason for limiting the cross-border mobility of workers. in conclusion, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mrs rie oomen-ruijten, who has done an incredible job, and i hope that the solutions contained in this report will also improve the situation on the labour market.
for many years, the commission has been warning that few citizens are exercising their right to seek employment in the single market. recent figures show that only 3% of our citizens live in a country other than their country of origin, which is proof that the free movement of workers is not working as we would like it to. the reasons for this are many, one of them being undoubtedly the difficulties in maintaining entitlements to supplementary pensions. they are increasingly popular and, given the difficulties with pension systems in most member states, their importance will certainly increase. this act should therefore be supported. the compromise reached between parliament and the council is a step in the right direction: on the one hand, it allows the existing problems, especially those resulting from relatively short periods of work in another member state, to be solved, linked to the extremely popular wave of migration, and on the other hand it seeks to take account of the existing differences between member states in the functioning of supplementary pension and pension schemes. however, it is important that the measures introduced are properly disseminated to migrant workers. the practice shows that many of the solutions adopted at european level do not work simply because citizens are unaware of their existence. it will therefore be for the commission to ensure that the directive's requirements for informing workers are implemented at all levels, from the member states to the workers. i would like to thank very warmly the rapporteur, riia oomen-ruijten, for her commitment to the subject of pensions in the european parliament. thanks to her determination over many years, we have been able to complete a lot of work on this dossier and most importantly to introduce many valuable solutions. thank you so much for your job!
madam president, as a member of the european parliament, i have directed many of my efforts towards improving the situation of europe’s senior citizens. many of them live on a fixed income, often in the form of a state pension. however, the question of pension rights is not limited to the elderly. virtually all europeans will one day retire and start collecting social benefits. pension rights are an especially important topic in these times of precarious employment, economic difficulties and demographic changes. many europeans – including myself in the past – travel across the continent in search of gainful employment. increasing work mobility has always been among the tenets of european integration; yet, now that we are closer than ever to realising this goal, disparaging voices arise across europe. we should not heed these detractors, but we should go on working towards creating a unified, pan-european labour market. simplifying and enhancing the process of the acquisition and preservation of supplementary pension rights is an important step towards this goal. i fully support this proposal and hope that it will help all europeans working abroad. i firmly believe that every person, no matter where he or she comes from, has the right to an adequate pension and a restful retirement.
the rapporteur. - madam president! - what are you doing? the freedom to provide services is one of the fundamental elements of european integration. it allows european companies to take advantage of the opportunities offered by the single market and thus create jobs and growth, which are particularly needed in the wake of the crisis. under this freedom in the european union, businesses from both western and central and eastern europe post around one million workers a year to provide services in another member state, with 70% of the posted workers coming from western europe. one of the challenges of posting is to ensure that the rights of posted workers are adequately protected, while allowing companies to benefit from the opportunities to provide services in the internal market. the implementing directive we are discussing today aims to improve the implementation of the 1996 directive which contains the basic conditions necessary to be met in the event of a posting. the economic situation and the upcoming european parliament elections made the work on the implementing directive difficult but intensive. i have often been confronted in the european parliament with ideas aimed at eliminating this form of economic activity, which unfortunately was often dictated by purely protectionist considerations. the abolition of posting would have a very negative impact not only on the economy but also on the labour market, on workers who would lose jobs that are so much needed today. i am very pleased that we have managed to reach an agreement with the council which, in the view of the overwhelming majority of member states (25 countries voted in favour of the agreement) and the large majority of the committee on employment and social affairs (30 members voted in favour, 11 against, 3 abstentions), will help to improve the protection of workers' rights and ensure that businesses can benefit from the internal market. contrary to the rhetoric of some quarters, the implementing directive contains a number of provisions that will improve the protection of workers' rights. by introducing a clear list of elements characterising national posting, labour inspectorates will be able to detect cases of abuse and breaches of the law, such as 'postbox companies' or false employment, more quickly and efficiently. states will be obliged to provide adequate protection for workers in the event that the posting is found to have been unlawful. they will be required to set up a single national website with all the information on employment conditions in the host country, giving workers the opportunity to obtain information on what rights they have. workers will also have access to mechanisms to enable them to exercise their rights efficiently and quickly, such as payment of arrears, including remuneration. states will continue to be able to decide on the choice of control measures to be applied to companies that post workers, which will allow for the efficient and effective control and elimination of dishonest employers. in the construction sector, workers will be subject to a solidarity mechanism which will ensure that they are paid, inter alia, wages. the member states will be able to apply a similar mechanism to other sectors or more restrictive arrangements depending on the needs of the local market. the cross-border enforcement of penalties and fines imposed on dishonest companies has also been improved. the main emphasis on the part of the entrepreneurs is on ensuring legal clarity, the lack of which is the main problem preventing companies from complying adequately with the provisions of the 1996 directive. the introduction of a list of elements characterising posting will help companies to understand what additional responsibilities labour inspections have to fulfil. the obligation for member states to inform the european commission of their control measures and to publish information on control instruments on a single national website will give businesses legal clarity and certainty that they can meet the requirements of labour inspections. the solutions contained in the directive will significantly improve the situation of workers, streamlining the posting process which provides jobs to around one million workers a year, representing over 18% of those working in a member state other than their country of origin.

mr. chairman, please! it's a special day for me. this is my last speech here in the plenary. i am very happy and honoured to have worked with such wonderful people, the budgetary officers of the european parliament, who are here today, and i thank you again for all that i have learned from you. at the same time, it is a little sad that we are talking again in the same spirit as at the beginning of the mandate. there is not enough progress on own resources. we have a long way to go, but these reforms are necessary. why would you do that? in recent years, the european union has been enlarged by 12 new member states. the european union has acquired new competences, new responsibilities and new expectations of the european union. she's got new assignments, new areas of operation. at the same time, the system of financing the eu budget has remained virtually unchanged since the 1970s. customs revenue, once an important source of financing for the communities, now represents a small part of the revenue of the union budget. this is partly the result of the progressive liberalisation of international trade, which, ironically, is being promoted by the european union. for me, this is further proof that the union is a victim of its own success. currently, the majority of the funding is provided by membership fees. this, in my view, makes the union heavily dependent on the particular and short-term interests of the member states. the wider benefits of eu integration, such as the creation of an area of democracy, an area of civil liberties, peaceful conflict resolution, a common market, are in this debate, and i very much regret that they are being pushed to the back burner. i was saddened to learn that the council not only did not accept the european commission's proposal to introduce new types of own resources, but also further extended the system of membership rebates. the current system for financing eu expenditure is opaque and lacks independence from the political, often short-term, interests of the member states. it is often said that the last 40 years have seen enormous economic and social changes in europe and around the world. to ensure the smooth functioning of the union, we are obliged to reform the own resources system. new types of own resources need to be introduced, but above all the system needs to be simplified to make it fairer and more understandable to citizens. i am also convinced that a bold, open and honest debate is needed on the benefits of the european union for all member states.
in writing. – parliament’s push for reform on the system of the eu’s own resources has been constant throughout the negotiations on the eu’s multiannual financial framework (mff) 2014-20. in these negotiations, parliament backed the commission proposals, which suggested the abolition of the current vat resource and introduction of two new genuine own resources, replacing the current correction mechanisms with a new system of temporary corrections and a reduction to 10% in the share of traditional own resources that ms retain as collection costs. unfortunately, the council’s position only backed a reduction to 20% of ms collection costs on traditional own resources. it upheld the temporary correction mechanisms and decided that the introduction of a new vat resource to replace the existing one still requires further work. parliament expressed, on more than one occasion, disappointment with the council for not making more progress on the reform. the current system puts too much burden on ms national treasuries. it further causes a debate between ‘net receivers’ and ‘net beneficiaries’, which disregards the added value of the eu budget. the longer the council delays a reform, the longer it prevents a genuine, clear, simple and fair system of revenue collection.

in writing. - in today's vote i supported the amendment to the european parliament and council directive amending council directive 2001/110/ec because i agree with the view that pollen is a natural component of honey, not a constituent. given the process of production of honey, pollen is naturally present in honey, since it is introduced into the hive only by the bees and is present in the honeycomb completely independent of human activity. if we were to accept that pollen from genetically modified plants is a component of honey, this would lead to a significant increase in the price of this product and to the cessation of production by small-scale beekeepers. the costs of the tests that would have to be carried out to collect the information necessary for the labelling of honey would reduce the profitability of such production and, in addition, would mislead the consumer into believing that such pollen is added to honey at the production stage and that honey is no longer a fully natural product.
in writing. honey is a 100% natural product. pollen is not a component of honey, but a natural component of honey. the bees that collect the nectar carry the pollen, and that's where it's in the honey. recognising pollen as an ingredient of honey would mislead consumers who might think that pollen is added to honey. that's obviously not true. this regulation and the definition of pollen are of great importance for the beekeeping industry. if honey were to be labelled as containing genetically modified pollen, it would lose its reputation as a natural product and, consequently, its positive reputation among consumers. recognition of pollen as an ingredient would increase the cost of labelling studies. the costs would be most burdensome for small producers, as they could undermine the profitability of production. on the other hand, the increase in production costs will lead to an increase in retail prices for honey. the recognition of pollen as a natural component does not mean that labelling will not indicate that the pollen is genetically modified, if this is the case. if the amount of genetically modified pollen exceeds the threshold of 0,9% in the product, then the relevant annotation will appear on the label. i support the report by mrs girling, because we are acting to protect the market for honey producers. i would like to emphasise that the recognition of pollen as a component of honey will not have any harmful consequences for public health.

in writing. - new psychoactive substances which have been found to have a serious impact on public health must be subject to control. the so-called market creativity, i.e. the creation of new substances and their mixtures, is a continuous process. current european legislation does not regulate the control of these substances, so legislation is needed to cover substances that are on the market now and will be in the future. the production and distribution of psychoactive substances which are harmful to health must be prohibited and any infringement of this prohibition should be punished. this is the direction taken by the provisions set out in the report by mrs jimenez-becerril barrio. the minimum provisions establishing criminal penalties and sanctions in the field of illicit drug trafficking apply to persons and groups involved in the production and distribution of psychoactive substances that pose a threat to health. i support the report by mrs jimenez-becerril barrio and believe that any action to control and punish illegal activities involving psychoactive substances is essential. i believe that a precise directive setting out the characteristics of offences and penalties in the area of illicit trafficking in psychoactive substances is very much needed, and i therefore agree with the rapporteur. this is also my view in my opinion for the envi committee, which highlights the danger to public health of the uncontrolled entry of new psychoactive substances into the market.

madam president, while we should certainly look at the ttip from the point of view of the economic opportunities it will generate, it is also clear that its public perception matters strongly. ttip will be attracting a growing amount of public attention, and there are legitimate anxieties linked to it which will have to be addressed. but we must not see ttip as a simple sum of individual stakeholder interests. it is an unprecedented strategic deal between the largest economies and democracies of the world, with robust welfare growth and job consequences for the transatlantic citizen. it is a deal with significant global relevance. while the benefits from the deal will be more mid- to long-term, the confidence of the citizens needs to be earned today. this is also our responsibility in this house. it is up to us in the european parliament to reflect on how the critical mass of the benefits can be measured and it is also up to us in the european parliament to contribute, in a constructive way, to the final assessment of its added value.
madam president, a comprehensive agreement on trade liberalisation between the eu and the us is urgently needed, given the growing competitive pressures coming from emerging new powers such as china and india. the planned opening of markets offers important economic benefits. the ttip would increase the gdp of both partners by between about 0.5% and 1% if implemented fully. the agreement would also make sense for political reasons as it would consolidate the long-term strategic alliance between the eu and the us which is necessary to confront new risks and challenges in the era of globalisation and international conflicts. we must not miss this unique opportunity; removal of trade barriers is necessary to increase the competitiveness of european firms and to create new jobs in europe. of course there are also risks involved. the level of protection in areas such as personal data protection or health and veterinary standards should not be reduced. also transition periods should apply in sectors where us firms enjoy a large competitive advantage, but on balance this agreement deserves our support.
in writing. the entry into force of the ttip will create the world's largest trading area, which is undoubtedly a tempting argument for its early adoption. at the same time, it should be borne in mind that the agreement will cover not only market access but also investment protection, services, public procurement, non-tariff barriers and trade-related rules. the agreement is also likely to benefit eu industry estimated to bring in about €120 billion a year for the eu. for consumers, the agreement means cheaper products, especially electronics, which are still eagerly imported from the us. however, market opening risks lowering eu standards for consumer safety and employment conditions. the ttip is also often compared to acta, due to the high risk of insufficient protection of personal data for eu citizens. the most questionable mechanism is known as 'investor-state dispute settlement' (isds), a provision in international trade agreements that gives an investor the right to bring proceedings against the state in which it has business. the negotiations on ttip are also not facilitated by the trail of the nsa's spying programmes in the eu. in view of the above concerns, it is important to establish the conditions without which the contract cannot be accepted (protection of personal data, workers' rights, transparency of the negotiation process).
in writing. as the european parliament, we should, within our powers, strongly support the negotiating process for the transatlantic trade and investment partnership between the eu and the us and monitor its progress on an ongoing basis to ensure tangible benefits for citizens. the removal of barriers to trade and investment will undoubtedly translate into economic growth in both europe and the americas. it will also have a positive impact on the global economy. the agreement should be structured in such a way that its provisions in the future contribute to the creation of more jobs, to the improvement of investment conditions and to the reduction of administrative burdens. ttip has the potential to bring many tangible benefits to ordinary citizens and european businesses: lower prices for online purchases, easier access for smes to the us market, and increased exports to the us. the agreement could also have a positive impact on improving europe's energy security. gas prices from the united states could be reduced, and access to innovative energy technologies would also be improved. for the agreement to deliver all these benefits, it is necessary to take due account of differences between the eu and the us in production costs, legislation, production processes and economic and social conditions. the eu and the us have a very strong chance of improving economic growth and the labour market. i hope we use it properly.
in writing. a year has passed since eu and us representatives began negotiations on the transatlantic trade and investment partnership (ttip). now, the enthusiasm for this deal is much less than it was a year ago. on both sides of the atlantic, there is growing resistance from some social groups. the growing resistance to ttip in both europe and the us is largely due to the disillusionment of some sections of society with the process of globalisation, which has benefited mainly large corporations, and both economies have experienced deindustrialisation. in europe, there are also concerns about differences in labour costs in favour of americans using cheap latin american labour and more than twice as cheap energy in the us. in the eu, we also have serious concerns about maintaining our highest standards in the world for food production and animal welfare. the american "we" is the import of hormone-laced meat, chlorine-laced poultry, and the invasion of genetically modified foods. in addition, in the area of intellectual property rights, we are in favour of maintaining european geographical indications which guarantee that the interests of our producers are protected. the trade and investment agreement is clearly needed by both sides, which are facing increasing economic pressure from new powers such as china, india and brazil. the creation of a transatlantic free trade area can bring further growth in trade and investment on both sides of the atlantic.
madam president! the european union, including poland, is experiencing a serious demographic crisis. the fertility rate in poland is one of the lowest in the world at 1.3, placing my country 212 out of 224. for law and justice, the party i represent, family-friendly policies are an essential pillar of social policy. we believe that family policy should be a matter of common concern through funding from the european social fund, while action to strengthen families, their sustainability and economic independence should be the responsibility of the nation states. the directive on minimum maternity leave promotes many good solutions. efforts should be made to provide effective support for motherhood and fatherhood. it is time for europe to tackle the demographic crisis not with words but with real action.
madam president! for years we have been involved in the european union's struggle to ensure equal treatment for men and women, with a number of fair but often forced solutions. but we should realize that there is one biological relationship that women should have greater legal protection through - and that is motherhood. in the light of the major demographic problems that many regions of europe are facing today, should we not see motherhood as one of the social investments whose costs are shared across society, in the form of more day-care centres, kindergartens or schools and activities for children, complemented by legal protection for women in terms of labour law? the conclusions of the june council meeting on women and the economy contain provisions on gender equality in the light of equal responsibility for children and domestic work, with emphasis on paternity leave and flexible childcare. these are not issues that can be delayed, especially in the context of the employment crisis among young people, including women, for whom the current situation is leading to an increasingly late maternity and sometimes to a complete abandonment of it. i hope that the commissioner's declaration today on the preparation of new solutions will ensure that they are reasonable and sound.

madam president! as one of the measures to tackle youth unemployment, it is proposed to increase the transnational mobility of workers, which is of course in the interest of those countries which like germany suffer from a lack of labour. freedom of movement and settlement is a great achievement of europe. and i'm not in favor of closing the borders, as some of my colleagues here are. but we must also be aware of the impact of migration on the countries from which young people leave. this is the case in many central and eastern european countries, for example poland, where more than 2 million people, mostly young people, have left since 2004. if it weren't for this emigration, unemployment would be much higher. but the departure of young people is deepening the demographic crisis, contributing to economic and political stagnation, and robbing these societies of their dynamism. moreover, immigrants often work much below their qualifications, often in conditions that are not worthy of the standards of the country in which they live. another reason for emigration is the desire to start a family, which young people cannot afford in their own country. the european union has a long-term strategy for the future, and it is not just the european union that is facing this challenge. it is only a confirmation of the inequality between european countries. i ask that all programmes for youth employment also take this aspect into account.

acting president of the council, on behalf of the vice-president of the commission and high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, tomorrow, 17 july, is the international day of justice, which coincides with the 16th anniversary of the rome statute of the international criminal court, which was adopted on 17 july 1998. with the rome statute the world has consolidated its historic commitment to prevent and deter the most heinous crimes. the implementation of this promise of justice for the victims of crimes under the rome statute is a moral imperative and at the same time an essential contribution to peace, security and well-being in the world. today the international criminal court is the backbone of the international criminal justice system and an important instrument for holding to account those responsible for the most serious crimes of international concern. the eu, as is well known, has a strong tradition of strong support for the international criminal court. we believe that the international community finds an efficient court of justice to be an indispensable instrument in combating impunity and promoting an international order based on the rule of law. the international criminal court will remain an important priority for the european union in the years to come. we therefore welcome the debate in plenary today on the crime of aggression. the active involvement of the european parliament in this important issue for human rights and international justice is essential. the rome statute review conference, held in kampala, uganda, from 31 may to 10 june 2010, marked a milestone by providing a forum for states, international organisations and civil society representatives in kampala to reaffirm their commitment to promoting the statute and to taking stock of international criminal justice, but not only. the kampala review conference also marked an important step in the consolidation of the international criminal court as an effective instrument by which the international community brings to justice those criminally responsible for crimes under the rome statute when national courts are unable or unwilling to prosecute them. the review conference adopted important amendments to the rome statute, including the definition of the crime of aggression and the conditions under which the international criminal court can exercise jurisdiction in this matter. the amendment must now be ratified or accepted by the states parties to the rome statute. provided that a sufficient number of ratifications are made and that a two-thirds majority of states adopt a decision to that effect after 1 january 2017, the international criminal court will be able to exercise jurisdiction over the crime of aggression. as this parliament is aware, all the member states of the european union are parties to the statute and some have even already ratified the kampala amendment on the crime of aggression. in others, however, the ratification process is in its final stages or at any rate advanced, while others have indicated that they do not intend to ratify this amendment at the moment. the european union cannot ratify the amendment as it is not itself a party to the rome statute. however, with the facilitation of the european external action service, the member states of the european union exchange information and, where appropriate, coordinate on the progress of the ratification process. our common goal in this process is clear: further strengthen the court to fulfil its mandate. the rome statute is a promise to the victims of the worst atrocities in the world, a promise that they will get justice, a promise that by seeing the guilty face up to their responsibilities, the affected communities will be able to move beyond violence to peace, from lawlessness to the rule of law. few of us could have foreseen, ten years ago, that the court would become the focal point of all discussions on the fight against impunity. few of us imagined, ten years ago, that the court would be able to prosecute crimes committed in 15 countries spanning three continents. but many have worked towards this goal and welcome the results achieved, both in the parliaments and in the european parliament. today's debate on the crime of aggression illustrates once again how, within the framework of the rome statute, the institutional criminal court continues to play, together with national courts, an essential role in ensuring justice for the victims of the most heinous crimes.
on behalf of the ppe group. we have had the opportunity on many occasions, in particular in the subcommittee on human rights, to hear updates on the functioning of the international criminal court. we have also made some recommendations to strengthen the role of the court and all the activities in which the european union could support the court. the kampala amendment to the rome statute defines the concept of the crime of aggression, which is to be subject to the jurisdiction of the international criminal court. to do so, these amendments must be ratified by at least 30 countries. so far, as we note in the resolution we will be voting on tomorrow, it has been ratified by 14 countries, including 8 member states of the european union. i hope that in the near future there will be more of these countries, including my own country, poland, which is already in the final stages of the ratification process. the crime of aggression is invading another country, but also firing at it, blocking its ports. aggression can be carried out by either a regular army or by supporting irregular armed forces on the territory of another state. i am convinced that if these amendments had been enacted a few years ago, perhaps we could have avoided at least some of the conflicts that have occurred since then, and thus, most importantly, we could have avoided a lot of human suffering and a lot of national tragedy. tomorrow is world justice day. i think that the adoption of this resolution calling for the swift completion of the ratification process by those states that accept the kampala amendments would be a very important step on that day.
on behalf of the ecr group. - madam president! - i have to go. aggression is historically considered the most important crime under international law. it also often provides the means or even the impetus for further international crimes, such as war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity. the international community needs a universal legal definition of aggression, because unfortunately, we don't have one. the london conventions of 1933, which formulated such a legal definition, are binding on only about 10 countries, including my own poland. unfortunately, only in their relationship. in contrast, un general assembly resolution 3314 of 1974, which is universal, like all un general assembly resolutions, is not a legally binding definition. the adoption of the kampala amendment to the icc statute will therefore create a new quality, equip this court with the ability to punish the perpetrators of aggression and give us a legal definition that will be binding. at the same time, it will be adopted as a target model by a large part of the international community. but let us not forget that today, on the basis of universal jurisdiction, the perpetrators of the crime of aggression can be punished in this way by national courts, not only their own, but also by international criminal tribunals ad hoc, established after the crime of aggression or other international crimes. let's take advantage of that opportunity.

rapporteur. - mr president, i am hereby submitting to the european parliament the legislative proposal to ratify – to give consent to – the association agreement between the european union and the ukraine, ten years after the orange revolution, which deceived so many hopes, one year after the failure in vilnius to sign the association agreement and 10 months after the beginning of the heroic and victorious euromaidan, which was a sign of the wish and will of the ukrainian nation to make its european choice. the european choice of ukraine, through this ratification today, will be institutionalised in the form of an association agreement and will in future bind the european union and the ukraine together. during the past 10 months, ukrainian citizens proved to be committed to european values and willing to fight for the country’s democratic development. ukrainian society has paid the highest price for their european aspirations, grieving the deaths of numerous people, suffering territorial occupation by russia and experiencing a deteriorating economic situation. the european union was extending assistance to the ukrainian state. from the eu side the eu has assisted ukraine economically and politically and with this ratification it gives ukraine the strongest sign of support. economic support on the union’s side is substantial, with a financial package amounting to up to eur 11 billion, and it also covers political support, which is embodied in the creation of the support group for ukraine in the european commission, the organisation of the international donors conference and efforts towards establishment of the technical assistance plan in a number of areas, from constitutional to judicial and administrative reform. this ratification is a milestone rapporteur. - mr president, i am certain that in a few minutes this house will, with a great majority, ratify the association agreement between the european union and ukraine, thus sending a strong signal of support and solidarity. the association agreement can provisionally enter into force immediately after reciprocal notification by both sides of the ratification and it will mean work in secret by commissioner de gucht as to how to make it half enter into force – politically but not economically. after ratification the association agreement – and this is the formal statement of the rapporteur and of the forthcoming resolution – cannot be changed by one word or one comma. we have to do all we can in order to prevent it being stopped or derailed. our moscow sources say that a letter demanding changes to the text has already been sent to commissioner de gucht from russia. i believe that with our ratification we are completely closing the gate to such possibilities and that we are acting in accordance with all the elements of our resolution, which is to be put to the vote on thursday, that demand further, more audacious, extended and enhanced action by the european union to assist ukraine in its economic and political process and also in the defence of its territorial integrity and, ultimately, of the dignity of the ukrainian nation.
in writing. - the eu-ukraine association agreement adopted by the ep is a support for ukraine's independence and unity. the agreement covers both political and economic aspects of cooperation. policy support will cover areas such as energy and transport. the agreement with ukraine also includes a commitment to a series of reforms and to respect for the principles of democracy and human rights. the agreement also introduces the principle of free trade, which will allow for a deeper integration of the ukrainian market with the eu market. in the absence of an effective solution to the russian-ukrainian conflict, ukraine's integration into the eu offers a chance to protect against further russian expansion. the eu's own history shows the importance of broad economic cooperation for peace. there is no doubt that the eu and ukraine have a common interest in the stability of the eu's eastern border. despite strong support from meps in a vote of 535 to 535, the agreement has yet to be ratified by 28 member states. only four countries have ratified it so far.

and promote human rights and to support democracy around the world. the european union has put human rights at the very centre of its external action and is undoubtedly one of the main international actors in the field. one of the reasons for this is the leading role played by the european parliament in influencing and shaping our democracy and human rights policy. i would like to praise the work raised in the document are taken up in our annual report. this proves that in the protection and promotion of human rights and democracy we stand united. since the adoption of the human rights package appreciated this effort to provide transparency and accountability. allow me a few words on the strategic framework and action plan on human rights and democracy. the adoption of this package was a landmark decision. it provided us with a clear set of principles and objectives to guide our work in promoting human rights in the world. thanks to these comprehensive documents, the eu’s delivery has become more tangible and more measurable. it has also made our endeavours part of a collective effort involving all eu institutions and member states alike. i am pleased to say that, in two years, we have accomplished most of the nearly 100 actions set out, and we are working on completing the remaining ones. at a time when democratic values are increasingly being challenged in many parts of the world, the high representative and her services, including eu delegations, have addressed human rights and democracy as a matter of priority. those who are oppressed around the world, as well as civil society representatives and international partners, look up to the european union and count on our contribution. the eu has not feared to go beyond traditional diplomacy and to express its concerns openly. baroness ashton did just that over the developments in russia in relation to civil society. she spoke out on the harassment of civil society in latin america and sub-saharan africa. she called for the release of political prisoners in bahrain while attending the eu and gulf cooperation council ministerial meeting. in myanmar she joined aung san suu kyi in attending a special civil society forum with more than 60 participants from all parts of the country. civil society representatives were similarly involved in the eu-myanmar/burma task force and participated actively in its political session. the role of stavros lambrinidis as the eu’s special representative for human rights has also been crucial. throughout these past two years he has shown incredible stamina and has spared no efforts in designing and projecting our human rights policy across the world and in advancing the universality of human rights. he has been, and is constantly, engaging with all our strategic partners and has consistently addressed human rights challenges with key countries in democratic transition. he has been, and still is, tirelessly reaching out to ngos and civil society organisations. stavros has proved to be the eu’s solid and loud voice on human rights. our eu annual report sets out a number of our key achievements. we have moved forward with our human rights country strategies: we have now concluded more than 150 strategies, covering the globe and providing tailor-made approaches and strategic objectives for each individual country. this has been an important step in empowering our eu delegations in their new post-lisbon role. in addition, we have established human rights focal points in all eu delegations and common security and defence policy missions and operations. we have stepped up efforts to train our staff on human rights and democracy issues, both in the delegations and at headquarters. every year the union holds human rights dialogues and consultations with more than 30 partner countries and regional groupings. in 2013, human rights dialogues with south africa and burma/myanmar and consultations with the republic of korea were held for the first time. we have extended our toolkit by adopting new eu human rights guidelines. in 2013 we adopted guidelines to promote and protect the enjoyment of all human rights by lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intra-sex persons, as well as guidelines on freedom of expression freedom of belief, following the adoption by this house of a detailed recommendation on the topic. we have promptly condemned cases of religious hatred, intolerance and violence in the world: in egypt, nigeria, iran, libya, mali, pakistan and tunisia and, more notably, following the tragic developments unfolding in iraq and syria. at the same time, all our instruments – political dialogues, démarches, technical assistance and support for ngos – are used to address more systematic issues related to freedom of religion or belief in a bilateral context. conscious of the increased incidence of intimidation and harassment of journalists and of restrictions on media freedom, we adopted a few months ago the first ever guidelines on freedom of expression online and offline, in consultation with civil society and under the inspiration of parliament’s report on the freedom of press and media in the world. at the same time, the eu has loudly condemned attacks on journalists and bloggers, and has participated in all international efforts to promote and protect freedom of expression. the eu has used all its available tools of diplomacy and cooperation and assistance to work towards the abolition of the death penalty. we have issued hundreds of statements and carried out hundreds of démarches to condemn the use of capital punishment wherever and whenever it occurs. thanks to our constant efforts and lobbying, the un general assembly 67th session adopted a resolution on a moratorium on executions, with unprecedented support. thanks to our efforts, no european drugs are exported to states that use lethal injections to execute. as we approach the 30th anniversary of the adoption of the un convention against torture, the eu has stepped up its efforts to address this unacceptable practice, which still exists in so many countries around the world. the eu has shown an equally active commitment to combating discrimination, especially discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity. we have never refrained from stating our belief that all people are created equal and that no cultural, societal or religious traditions can be invoked to justify any form of discrimination. gender has always been a top priority. the eu has taken an active stance on the elimination and prevention of all forms of violence against women and girls. thanks to our outreach, we were able to contribute to the successful adoption of conclusions at the 57th session of the un commission on the status of women. our strong engagement has also yielded results in the implementation of un security council resolution 1325 on women, peace and security. the protection and the promotion of children’s rights and the issue of children and armed conflict have been central to the eu human rights policy and funding instruments. the eu is proud to support the campaign, children, not soldiers, jointly initiated in 2014 by the un special representative for children and armed conflict and unicef, aiming to end and prevent the recruitment and use of children in conflict by 2016. supporting civil society has remained at the heart of our objectives. we continue to focus on protecting ngos and human rights defenders and expanding the space in which they operate. we have called on numerous governments to make sure that new legislation is adopted and implemented in line with international standards. human rights defenders play an important role at local, national, regional and international levels, and the promotion of human rights cannot exist without them. this year the eu celebrated the 10th anniversary of its guidelines on human rights defenders. through various instruments, such as small grants and ‘sheltered cities’, the eu has actively illustrated its support for vulnerable and marginalised human rights defenders. eu and member state diplomats on the ground have attended the trials of human rights defenders and made efforts to secure their release. a recent trial observation in saudi arabia is just one example. over the years, the eu has supported electoral processes throughout the world. since 2000 we have deployed 140 election observation missions. as in so many other fields, strong cooperation with parliament is all the more apparent here. at a multilateral level the eu remained active and engaged with all major international and regional partners. in recent years we have stepped up our cooperation with the council of europe, the osce and other regional mechanisms working on human rights. we intensified and advanced our agenda in geneva and new york. the eu’s role has been pivotal in key united nations achievements such as mandates for special rapporteurs and country resolutions from belarus, iran, burma/myanmar, the democratic people’s republic of korea and syria. i am looking forward to the debate on this important report and i look forward to your further contribution to the promotion of human rights in the world.

in writing. ladies and gentlemen! i come from a region that has experienced repeated flooding. my hometown of opole, in 1997 was almost completely flooded by the odra, and i will remember this experience for the rest of my life. i know the devastation that the rivers cause, and i understand the plight of those affected by this disaster. these experiences point to a number of significant problems. first, flood infrastructure requires river management, often destroying a unique natural environment. in poland, we are often faced with the dilemma of protecting our livestock or protecting endangered species, which often delays necessary investments for many years. secondly, effective flood management requires close cooperation between neighbouring countries. in europe, rivers are very rarely entirely within the borders of one country. thus, the actions of one country can make or break the situation in another. the flood risk management plans required by the flood directive have not yet been drawn up, and their implementation will show whether we can work together effectively. the experience of the past few years is not optimistic. however, it is to be hoped that both cooperation between member states and the ability to rapidly develop flood protection infrastructure will improve over time. we must remember that climate change will increase the frequency of floods and other disasters.

in writing. youth unemployment is a topic that is raised at every plenary session of the current term. and rightly so, for this is one of the most serious problems facing europe today. the youth guarantee is not a sufficient measure to address this problem, but it is an important instrument that can provide significant support for structural reforms undertaken by member states. however, their implementation must be accelerated. this appropriation is intended to cover the financing of the european schools for the period 2014-2020 (article 21 of the financial regulation). but that's not all. the only way to end unemployment permanently is to create new jobs. we need to stimulate economic growth, because only then will we create a good business climate. employers who have had to reduce their workforce as a result of the crisis must be provided with the right conditions to restore those jobs. we also need to encourage young people to be entrepreneurs and to create opportunities for them to start their own businesses. the support system must be comprehensive and include both administrative facilities and access to finance.
in writing. unemployment in the european union is slowly declining thanks to efforts at european and national level. however, the pace and scale of these efforts are still insufficient. the funds earmarked for the youth guarantee are being spent slowly and the implementation of policies to tackle unemployment in the member states is slow. it is clear that reducing unemployment requires not only training programmes and funding of employment agencies, but also deep structural reforms in both the vocational training system and the functioning of small and medium-sized enterprises, which provide the most jobs and are responsible for the largest share of income. during the debate, many people stressed that to achieve a lasting effect, the fight against unemployment must address its causes, not just its symptoms. for employment initiatives to be effective and to deliver on the eu's 75% employment target for 20-64 year olds, member states need public investment to encourage smes to create new jobs. the lack of growth will in the long term deepen the labour market crisis. the youth guarantee will not replace macroeconomic instruments which work across the market, improving not only the situation of young people but also that of older workers whose experience and skills are as important for the development of europe as the enthusiasm and modern education of young people.
in writing. the high level of youth unemployment remains a major problem in the union, and despite a downward trend, it remains high in some member states. in this context, effective monitoring and exchange of best practices on the implementation of the youth guarantee and on strategies to combat unemployment at european level is key. another issue is the rise in the number of long-term unemployed. according to 2014 statistics, almost 13 million people have been unemployed for more than a year, and more than one third of the unemployed have been unemployed for more than two years. long-term unemployment has negative consequences both for the long-term unemployed and for member states' budgets. the cost of keeping people out of work is estimated at pln 10.5 billion a year in poland, for example. however, most of the competence relating to employment lies with the member states, and therefore many aspects necessary for increasing employment are their responsibility. the necessary actions include the correlation of education systems with labour market needs to facilitate the transition from education to employment and the development of a knowledge-based economy.
the next item is the report by mr philippe de backer, drawn up on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the european semester for economic policy coordination: implementation of priorities for 2014 (2014/2059(ini)) (a8-0019/2014).
on behalf of the ppe group. – mr president, the european semester is an important component of the system of economic governance in the eu. its key instruments are country-specific recommendations (csrs) that aim at ensuring better coordination of economic policies and fostering crucial structural reforms in the member states. however, the overall effectiveness of csrs is still limited. only 10 to 15% of csrs have been fully implemented by member states in 2013. as a result, macroeconomic imbalances still persist, progress in implementing badly needed structural reforms is slow and uneven and strong economic growth in europe is still to come. in the report, the european parliament calls on the member states to undertake more effort to fully implement csrs. what is at stake is the very credibility of the european union and its ability to definitively overcome the current crisis. one way to improve the efficiency of the european semester is to make sure that reasons and causes for unsatisfactory implementation of csrs are properly analysed and eliminated and that the whole elimination process is more disciplined. another way is to radically strengthen national ownership of csrs in individual member states in order to mobilise sufficient political capital in favour of reforms. more involvement by national parliaments could also help. it would also improve democratic control over the whole exercise. in the process of preparing this report, a wide range of proposals and amendments have been submitted and discussed. we eventually managed to come up with a draft that represents a reasonable compromise and which reflects most of the key priorities of major political groups. therefore, i call on all member states and all members of the house to vote in favour of the report. we, as the european parliament, should support the european commission in its efforts to fully use the framework of the european semester to improve economic governance in europe.
mr. chairman, please! the european semester report is an important debate on the current state of the economies of the european union and their needs. i agree with many of the problems highlighted in the report, such as the issue of youth unemployment or the energy dependence of some european union countries, including my own country, on russia, but i cannot support the call for such far-reaching synchronisation of economic policies, which in the long term will be a threat to the sovereign budgetary policies of the member states. i am also concerned about the record of support for all three pillars of the banking union, which i oppose, and the call for a unified external representation of the euro area. i think we should leave more decision-making to the member states.
mr president, alongside budgetary macroeconomic measures, structural reforms are at the heart of the european semester, and the country-specific recommendations help identify the most pressing structural reform needs across europe. but what we need today is a strong structural reform commitment catalyst and coordination technology that would guide the reforms from the commitment stage to reality. the european commission enjoys as never before the legitimacy of both parliament and the council, and has the capacity and resources to coordinate and scrutinise structural reforms. so, unless the commission assumes this double role of commitment catalyst and coordination mechanism, the european debate on structural reform will remain empty rhetoric. markets will punish failure to act. europe, of course, cannot afford to run such a risk.
i'm closing the debate. the vote will take place on wednesday. the competent authority shall inform the applicant of the reasons for the refusal of the application.

we are in the midst of key decisions by the european council on the future of climate, energy policy, the future of our economic policy in the european union. the presidency has presented six climate policy objectives, but at the same time we as meps are asked: is it possible to reduce emissions by 40% while maintaining economic growth? will the new reduction targets allow, among other things, the rebuilding of jobs: the 5 million we are talking about in the europe 2020 strategy? will they also allow for the industry to gain from the re-industrialization a gdp growth of between 16% and 20%? that is the aim of the new commission. will the new reduction targets not lead to carbon leakage production diversion and also emissions outside the union and thus possibly also to capacity reductions in individual member states and their economies? how will we compete under the new free trade agreement with the united states, given that energy prices in the union are higher, that the united states is growing by more than 4% and that energy prices are lower, for example because of shale gas prices? how can we solve the energy supply problem (gas is one of the elements of reducing emissions, including imported gas) when energy has become a field and a weapon of confrontation, as evidenced by the conflict between russia and ukraine? i'd like to say that we have different goals. we want to achieve reductions, increase renewables, efficiency, and also make a good impression at cop21, but we also want to maintain energy prices and the number of emission allowances, for example, because of the crisis that has occurred. the general dispute is the height of the reduction targets and the division between countries, and maybe the countries that can reduce more should do more, and the others should do more, depending on their economic and social capabilities. member states - and this is my last point, mr president - should have the right to choose the path to reaching reduction targets, the amount of res and the implementation of energy efficiency. one size fits all approach should not be pushed.

in writing. in the context of the debate on the amendment of protocol 31 to the eea agreement on cooperation in the field of free movement of workers, coordination of social security systems and measures to assist migrants, including migrants from third countries, i draw attention to the need to respect the principle of free movement of workers. this key principle, which more than half of eu citizens consider to be the greatest achievement of european integration, has recently become too often the subject of national political games. such actions undermine the credibility of the eu project and create anti-migrant sentiment among local communities. it is also important to emphasise that immigrants not only do not overburden social security systems, but they mainly contribute to the economic growth of the country of immigration. we also have to bear in mind that there are over 2 million job vacancies in the union, so mobility, especially in regions with labour shortages and skills mismatches, is essential for their development. action to ensure that union citizens benefit from the principle of free movement is also crucial. almost half of migrant citizens complain of administrative obstacles related to the lack of knowledge of eu law on free movement among local government employees. europe needs growth and jobs. so instead of undermining the principle of free movement, we need to focus on fighting unemployment and stimulating investment that will create jobs.

in writing. the europe 2020 strategy lists among its objectives an increase in the employment rate to 75%. this will be difficult to achieve, as the value of this indicator has been hovering around 69% for several years, showing very weak upward trends. it is composed of 75% of the employment rate for men and 63% of the employment rate for women. there is thus a 12% employment gap between women and men, which in some member states is as high as 30% and is responsible for 40% of the gender pension gap in europe and poverty among older women. closing the employment gap, increasing the participation of women in the labour market is an effective way not only to achieve rapid economic growth, but also to achieve greater social justice in europe. recent years have shown that employment growth in the member states is mainly driven by the increase in the employment of women and that the implementation of the principle of gender equality is key to this process. women are statistically better educated and motivated to work than men but the barriers that block their access to the market must eventually be removed. gender equality needs to be promoted more effectively. nurseries, kindergartens, care homes, equal distribution of responsibilities in unpaid domestic work, closing the labour market gap are all necessary conditions for increasing the presence of women in the market and thus for smart and sustainable economic growth in europe.
in writing. – creating one european railway space is important to our economy. still, there are too many technical and administrative differences between the railways in europe – not mentioning the infrastructure bottlenecks we face at border crossings – such as between germany and poland. technical issues like different mobile equipment used by the railways in europe, such as pkk or sncf in france, create difficulties for locomotives to change from one ‘national’ railway system to the other. therefore i fully supported this convention and voted in favour. in order to create one european railway space we need to have the same technical standards for all of the european railways.
in writing. - i support the accession of the european union to the so-called railway protocol to the convention on international safety of mobile equipment. the main objective of the facility is to facilitate the financing of high-value rolling stock by providing a particularly strong international guarantee to creditors. the seller on credit (and the institutions providing credit for such sales) will be entitled to a security giving 'absolute priority' to such equipment entered in the newly established international register. it will be a system that guarantees the ability to search for established safeguards from anywhere in the eu using the internet, which means that the register will be available 24 hours a day. such an instrument will certainly bring great benefits and contribute to the development of the european railway industry, including the enterprises operating in the kujawsko-pomorskie region of poland, which are engaged in the production and repair of railway vehicles for rail transport.

in writing. - the start of the new ep term is the right moment to set global, unified development priorities and the direction eu policy should take. looking back at the millennium development goals set by the united nations in 2000, it makes perfect sense to do so: progress in the fight against certain diseases, and increased intergovernmental and interinstitutional cooperation are clear examples of the effectiveness of such declarations. discussions on the way forward have been intensified within the open working group on the sustainable development goals and the un intergovernmental panel of experts on sustainable development finance, and the position of the european commission, the eu council and the european parliament on the post-2015 agenda has been set out in a communication entitled 'a decent life for all'. the report by our colleague from the committee on development is the european parliament's contribution to creating a coherent, uniform framework for future action. these include, of course, such important issues as sustainable development, the elimination of social disparities, conflict prevention, adequate education and access to health care. however, sustainable agriculture and food security should not be forgotten, as these issues should be at the heart of any effort to eradicate poverty and improve the quality of life for all people on our planet.
in writing. the objective of the report on the eu and the global development framework after 2015 for which i voted is to set out a coherent eu development policy strategy for the period after 2015. the report is a step towards an ambitious development agenda based on broad international partnership in tackling issues of global concern such as poverty, access to education and healthcare, and gender equality. the union's development policy is strongly oriented towards the protection of human rights and the promotion of an inclusive model of economic development based on diversity, which is both effective and equitable. as a member of the femm committee, i am particularly supportive of the call for women's empowerment to be a priority area of development policy. the elimination of violence against women and harmful practices such as forced marriage, honour killings and female genital mutilation is a prerequisite for promoting gender equality. the report says that nothing - including elements of religion, culture or tradition - can justify violence, thus embodying the spirit of the universality of human rights, which is also the basis of the council of europe convention on preventing and combating violence against women. the development framework proposed by the ep also promotes equal opportunities in education and the labour market as part of a fair and economically beneficial development strategy.

in writing. i can agree with the resolution's statement that climate change requires an urgent response. the question is, what is it? i don't agree that it's primarily human activity that's causing global warming, and that if we don't reduce greenhouse gas emissions, we're going to see a 5c rise by the end of the century. this is a blanket statement, based on the belief that the ipcc hypothesis has been proven. it is not possible, by accepting such an unproven claim, to simulate future climate effects by extrapolation. that is an incredibly crude, unscientific oversimplification. what should be the international response to global warming? first, we need to quickly and unequivocally determine whether the causes of these changes are natural or anthropogenic. second, if it turns out that the causes are anthropogenic, it is necessary to determine whether the causes are greenhouse gases or dust, or deforestation or other factors. third, more attention should be paid to the country-specific effects of climate change, as excessive focus on reducing co2 emissions is extremely costly and can delay or even prevent the equally costly and urgent need for countries to adapt to climate change. fourth, we need a broad discussion about climate change, its causes and local and global impacts, and that is not guaranteed by the ipcc and the belief in the infallibility of this unfortunate quasi-scientific body.

on behalf of the ecr group. - how are you, commissioner? i am delighted that we can join you today in this first debate on a major issue. the house will vote on wednesday on a draft implementing regulation on the classification of serious infringements of eu rules that may lead to the loss of good repute of a road haulage operator. at the last meeting of the transport committee, it was decided to refer this proposal back to the european commission for further development. i agree with the previous speakers and i hope that the european parliament will confirm this decision of the committee on transport on wednesday, which was already taken a few days ago. why would you do that? because the list presented is not complete and does not cover all the categories of infringements leading to the loss of the good reputation of transport operators, nor those which create a risk of serious injury to road users and the social expectations of drivers. the european commission's proposal is therefore unbalanced and consequently fails to take account of the interests of either employers or workers. we expect a more rational approach, a thorough analysis of the arguments of both sides and the safeguarding of their interests. the infringement catalogue should not in any way undermine the principle of subsidiarity or seek to eliminate road hauliers from the transport market. we need an expert debate and discussion today on the violations in the international road transport market. we must develop instruments which, on the one hand, counter illegal cabotage and, on the other, take account of the often rational arguments of drivers on social issues.
madam president! the regulation we are discussing today addresses the issue of breaches of reputation and loss of reputation by road hauliers. in my view, the commission has not precisely defined all the road safety offences and those who raise these doubts should be agreed. the delegated act should be complete, transparent and lead to better enforcement, rather than allowing for free interpretation and selective treatment. we have too many road accidents and the human tragedy that goes with them to be superficial. i therefore support those who say that the list of infringements should be supplemented. the debate on the regulation has also opened up another area of increasing controversy, which concerns cabotage and so-called social dumping. it should be stressed that cabotage matters are regulated by a separate regulation of the european parliament and of the council and that cabotage infringements do not constitute grounds for the loss of good repute of the carrier as they are not directly related to road safety. when we talk about social issues, we have to consider a few aspects. first, we have one european union, we have a common market, but we also have significant differences in wages for the same job in different countries of the european union. secondly, it must not be forgotten that workers and drivers from one eu or non-eu country are often employed under very different conditions and at much lower rates than in the eu country where they work. third, you cannot solve problems that are uncomfortable for one country or government at the expense of other countries. i agree that this is a very difficult and important subject, and therefore i believe that there is a need for an expert and fact-based discussion on the extent of the infringements occurring in the international road transport market and the development of common instruments that would counter the phenomenon of illegal cabotage.
ladies and gentlemen! road transport is the backbone of goods transport within the european union it accounts for over 70% of all transport and generates close to 2% of the eu's gdp. this shows that it is a kind of circulation of the single market, without which it would be difficult to speak of the free movement of goods. despite its importance to the european economy, many barriers to business in this sector persist. many restrictions prevent companies from competing with each other, which in turn increases the cost of transporting goods. it is estimated that the current legal situation results in losses of close to eur 50 million per year. the voices of some governments calling for further restrictions and possibilities for the provision of national transport services by operators from other member states are therefore surprising. if we want to stimulate the european economy, increase production and re-industrialize, we must create the best possible conditions for the transport of goods. no country can attract investors unless it can transport its manufactured goods quickly. the new list of major road transport regulations being discussed today by the european commission must be carefully thought out so as not to lead to the collapse of transport companies, and precise enough to prevent some member states from misinterpreting it. the use of excessive controls for protectionist purposes will not only weaken the implementation of the internal road transport market and lead to a loss of its potential, but will also create an antagonistic climate in the international provision of transport services. we all want to improve the skills of professional road hauliers and thus improve road safety in the eu. common rules for the classification of serious
